options.C: Brief seizure during class, client recovered quickly, emergency services not needed, and the team was informed
options.D: Start time, duration, first body part affected, movements observed, responsiveness, injuries and time to full recovery

explanation: The correct answer is D (Start time, duration, first body part affected, movements observed, responsiveness, injuries and time to full recovery): A useful seizure record is a factual description of what was seen: timing, onset, movements, awareness, injuries and recovery. Diagnosing the seizure type, naming a cause or recommending restrictions goes beyond what a witness can establish, and a vague summary leaves out details the neurologist needs.

question: A 70-year-old man begins a balance program after two recent falls at home. His physiotherapist explains that each week the exercises will be slightly harder, such as narrowing his stance and reducing hand support. Which training principle is being applied?

options.A: Reversibility, because balance improvements are lost quickly when training stops, so difficulty must increase daily
options.B: Individuality, because every client must follow the same standardized ladder of balance exercises from the clinic
options.C: Progressive overload, because gradually increasing the challenge drives continued adaptation of balance control
options.D: Specificity, because balance training must occur on the same surface where his falls took place

explanation: The correct answer is C (Progressive overload, because gradually increasing the challenge drives continued adaptation of balance control): Progressively raising task difficulty is progressive overload, which keeps stimulating adaptation. Specificity concerns task similarity, reversibility concerns loss of gains after stopping, and individuality means programs should differ between clients rather than follow a standard ladder.

question: A 52-year-old accountant has low back stiffness after sitting for hours at her workstation, with no neurological signs or red flags. Her employer has provided a height-adjustable desk, and she asks the physiotherapist how best to use it. Which approach is best supported?

options.A: Stand for two hours at a time, then sit for two hours, repeating through the day
options.B: Stand throughout the workday, because standing removes the mechanical load that sitting places on the spine
options.C: Sit with a lumbar roll and take one long stretching break at lunch to reset posture
options.D: Alternate sitting and standing in short blocks through the day, changing position before discomfort builds

explanation: The correct answer is D (Alternate sitting and standing in short blocks through the day, changing position before discomfort builds): Frequent short changes of position spread load across tissues and stop discomfort from building, which suits her stiffness. Standing all day only swaps one sustained posture for another. Two hour blocks and a single lunch break still leave her in long static postures.

question: A 66-year-old man is on day two after coronary artery bypass surgery through a median sternotomy. He has pain with coughing and avoids deep breaths. The physiotherapist teaches him to hug a pillow against his chest while coughing. What is the purpose of this technique?

options.A: It prevents the chest from rising so that breathing stays diaphragmatic during the cough
options.B: It supports the incision and reduces pain and sternal stress so he can cough more effectively
options.C: It keeps the shoulders relaxed and drawn forward, which expands the lower ribs during the cough
options.D: It increases chest wall resistance, which helps loosen secretions before the cough is attempted

explanation: The correct answer is B (It supports the incision and reduces pain and sternal stress so he can cough more effectively): Hugging a pillow splints the sternotomy, reducing pain and motion at the incision so he can cough effectively and breathe deeply. It is not used to change the breathing pattern, expand the ribs or loosen secretions. The benefit comes from support of the wound.

question: A 58-year-old man was extubated yesterday. During his physiotherapy session you hear a high-pitched, harsh sound on inspiration without a stethoscope, loudest over the neck. He is anxious, using accessory muscles and his saturation is 91 percent. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Give a reliever inhaler and reassess in ten minutes, because the sound is most likely bronchospasm
options.B: Lie him flat and perform chest percussion, because secretions in the trachea are causing the noise
options.C: Stop treatment, keep him upright and alert the nurse and physician, because stridor suggests airway narrowing
options.D: Continue treatment with deep breathing exercises, because the sound is probably a retained lung secretion

explanation: The correct answer is C (Stop treatment, keep him upright and alert the nurse and physician, because stridor suggests airway narrowing): Loud inspiratory stridor audible at the neck after extubation signals upper airway narrowing from swelling or laryngeal injury, which can progress quickly. Prompt medical help is needed. Wheeze from bronchospasm is mainly expiratory, and airway clearance does not treat upper airway obstruction.

question: A 35-year-old woman, twelve weeks postpartum, has a 4 cm diastasis with midline doming when she does a curl-up. She wants to return to crunches and planks for a fitness test next week. Her pelvic floor symptoms are mild. Which advice should the physiotherapist give?

options.A: Stop abdominal work and await surgical repair, because exercise cannot narrow a gap this size
options.B: Continue crunches while wearing an abdominal binder, because the binder closes the gap during effort
options.C: Practise planks daily to strengthen the rectus, because a stronger muscle pulls the edges together
options.D: Start with deep abdominal activation and graded loading, avoiding movements that dome until control improves

explanation: The correct answer is D (Start with deep abdominal activation and graded loading, avoiding movements that dome until control improves): Doming shows the abdominal wall cannot manage the load, so she builds deep abdominal control first and progresses loading only when she can perform movements without doming. A binder does not train the muscles, and crunches or planks that produce doming increase strain on the linea alba. Surgery is not the first step, since many gaps improve with training.

question: A 69-year-old widower recovering from a stroke will return to an apartment where he lives alone. The discharge team needs help arranging meal delivery, transportation to appointments, and information about subsidized housing supports. Which team member is best placed to lead this part of the discharge plan?

options.A: The dietitian, who assesses nutrition needs and coordinates community meal programs and transport services
options.B: The social worker, who assesses social and financial needs and connects clients with community programs
options.C: The speech-language pathologist, who assesses communication needs and connects clients with community support programs
options.D: The physiotherapist, who assesses mobility and arranges funding for subsidized housing and transportation supports

explanation: The correct answer is B (The social worker, who assesses social and financial needs and connects clients with community programs): Social workers specialize in social, financial and housing needs and know the community programs that meet them. The dietitian can advise on nutrition but does not usually organize transport or housing. The physiotherapist and speech-language pathologist contribute to the plan within their own areas.

question: A 36-year-old man, six weeks after a severe traumatic brain injury, has lost elbow flexion range on the right. The elbow is warm and swollen with firm tissue palpable at the end of range, and passive movement is painful and abruptly blocked. What should the physiotherapist do first?

options.A: Stop forceful passive stretching and report the findings to the physician for imaging and diagnosis
options.B: Switch to gentle active-assisted ranging within the pain-free arc and recheck swelling at the next visit
options.C: Apply sustained low-load stretching with heat, because contracture is the likely cause of lost range
options.D: Apply cold and compression, then reassess the elbow at the next session before changing the program

explanation: The correct answer is A (Stop forceful passive stretching and report the findings to the physician for imaging and diagnosis): Warmth, swelling, a firm end-feel and painful blocked movement after severe brain injury suggest heterotopic ossification, so forceful stretching stops and the physician arranges imaging. Stretching with heat assumes a simple contracture. Gentle ranging or cold and compression with later review delays medical investigation.

question: A physiotherapist who treats mostly children is selecting continuing education for the year. A self-reflection exercise showed uncertainty with pediatric developmental assessment, but she enjoys sport medicine courses and is offered free tickets to a sport conference. Which choice best reflects continuing competence principles?

options.A: Choose learning based on her identified gap in pediatric assessment, which matches her caseload
options.B: Choose a broad general course in practice management, because it applies to most clients she treats
options.C: Attend the free sport conference, because enjoyable learning is retained longest by adults
options.D: Follow a colleague's recommended course on a popular manual therapy technique, because peers know current practice

explanation: The correct answer is A (Choose learning based on her identified gap in pediatric assessment, which matches her caseload): Continuing competence is directed by the gaps found in reflection and by the needs of the caseload, so pediatric assessment is the priority. A general management course, an enjoyable conference and a colleague's popular technique may be useful but do not address the identified gap in the area where her clients are at risk.

question: A 69-year-old man with well-managed heart failure (NYHA class II) is cleared by his cardiologist for aquatic exercise to treat hip pain. The physiotherapist plans closer monitoring while he is immersed to chest level. What is the main reason for this additional monitoring?

options.A: Cold water at 28 degrees causes sudden heart rate acceleration that exceeds responses seen on land
options.B: Warm water causes widespread vasoconstriction, which raises blood pressure during sustained aerobic exercise sets
options.C: Hydrostatic pressure shifts blood centrally and increases preload, which can strain a compromised heart
options.D: Buoyancy removes the effort of body weight, which lowers cardiac output unpredictably during walking

explanation: The correct answer is C (Hydrostatic pressure shifts blood centrally and increases preload, which can strain a compromised heart): Immersion to chest level squeezes blood from the limbs into the central circulation, raising venous return, preload and stroke volume. A failing heart may not tolerate that added volume, so symptoms and vital signs are watched. The other explanations misstate how buoyancy, temperature and vessels behave.

question: A 66-year-old woman has chronic shoulder pain. Her chart notes a recently diagnosed metastatic lesion in the humerus under investigation. Her physician has not yet received the imaging report. She asks for ultrasound because it helped her last year. How should the physiotherapist respond?

options.A: Treat only the neck and scapular muscles, and apply gel with a sensation check
options.B: Withhold ultrasound over the area and discuss the lesion with her physician first
options.C: Apply continuous ultrasound at a low dose, because pain relief is the priority
options.D: Use pulsed low-intensity ultrasound instead, because non-thermal output is safe over tumours

explanation: The correct answer is B (Withhold ultrasound over the area and discuss the lesion with her physician first): Therapeutic ultrasound is contraindicated over known or suspected malignancy, and a metastatic lesion needs medical management before any modality. Changing the mode or dose does not remove the concern.

question: A 50-year-old man had a plate and six screws placed in his right tibia after a fracture eight months ago. The bone is healed, and he has ankle stiffness. The physiotherapist wants to warm the tissues before mobilization and reviews her warming options. Which method should she avoid over the implant?

options.A: A paraffin wax bath, because heat conducts into metal and warms the plate beyond tissue tolerance
options.B: Pulsed or continuous shortwave diathermy, because metal can concentrate heat and burn adjacent tissue
options.C: Continuous therapeutic ultrasound, because sound waves reflect off metal and overheat adjacent tissue
options.D: A moist hot pack, because metal beneath the skin heats quickly and burns the surrounding tissue

explanation: The correct answer is B (Pulsed or continuous shortwave diathermy, because metal can concentrate heat and burn adjacent tissue): Shortwave diathermy heats deep tissue with electromagnetic energy that metal implants can concentrate, so it is avoided over the plate. Ultrasound with a moving head is generally acceptable over healed metal, and wax and hot packs warm superficial tissue where the implant does not change heat delivery. The healed bone does not alter this precaution.

question: An interprofessional team recommends long-term care for an 84-year-old man with advanced dementia. His daughter wants him at home with home care. The physiotherapist's assessment shows he needs help with all transfers and constant supervision at night, which the daughter says she cannot provide. How should the physiotherapist respond?

options.A: Tell the daughter that long-term care is the only safe choice for him now
options.B: Support the daughter's wish and arrange home exercises, since family preferences determine discharge destination
options.C: Present the functional findings, and hold a family meeting to explore supports, options and risks
options.D: Leave the discussion to the physician and confine her role to recording the assessment

explanation: The correct answer is C (Present the functional findings, and hold a family meeting to explore supports, options and risks): The disagreement is best addressed by sharing objective functional findings and bringing the family and team together to discuss realistic supports, risks and alternatives. Simply endorsing the wish, telling the daughter there is only a single path, or stepping back from the conversation does not serve shared decision-making.

question: A 35-year-old Muslim man with a knee ligament sprain is fasting from dawn to sunset during Ramadan. At his mid-afternoon session he feels slightly light-headed but his resting vital signs are normal. He insists on continuing therapy and does not want to break his fast. What is the most appropriate plan?

options.A: Respect his decision to fast, lower the intensity, and offer an evening time after sunset
options.B: Continue the full planned program, because normal resting vital signs show he can exercise safely
options.C: Insist he break his fast before exercising, because dehydration would raise his risk of injury
options.D: Postpone therapy until Ramadan ends, because fasting and rehabilitation cannot be combined safely

explanation: The correct answer is A (Respect his decision to fast, lower the intensity, and offer an evening time after sunset): Culturally safe care respects a religious practice while managing the real risk, here by reducing load and shifting timing so he can exercise when he has eaten and drunk. Demanding that he break his fast overrides his beliefs, and full intensity ignores his light-headedness. Postponing for a month delays recovery that can be handled safely with simple adjustments.

question: A 26-year-old marathon runner reports deep groin pain that builds during long runs and eases with rest. Single-leg hopping reproduces the pain, and hip internal rotation at end range is painful. Resisted adduction is strong and painless, and the pubic symphysis is not tender. Which condition is most likely?

options.A: Adductor longus strain, because groin pain with running suggests a muscle tendon injury
options.B: Athletic pubalgia, because pain during exertion suggests an abdominal wall and pubic injury
options.C: Acetabular labral tear, because deep groin pain with rotation suggests intra-articular damage
options.D: Femoral neck stress injury, because hop provocation and painful rotation implicate bone loading

explanation: The correct answer is D (Femoral neck stress injury, because hop provocation and painful rotation implicate bone loading): Load-related groin pain that is reproduced by hopping in a high-mileage runner suggests a femoral neck stress injury, which needs imaging before further loading. Painless resisted adduction argues against adductor strain, and the absence of symphysis tenderness makes pubalgia less likely. A labral tear is more typically linked with catching or clicking and pain on flexion with internal rotation, rather than pain that builds with running load and is provoked by hopping.

question: A physiotherapist explains a proposed course of exercise-based treatment to a 47-year-old nurse with chronic shoulder pain. The nurse asks what information she must receive before she can agree to start. Which set of information is needed for her consent to be informed?

options.A: Nature of the treatment, expected benefits, material risks, alternatives, and the right to decline
options.B: Benefits, the treatment schedule, common side effects, and a signed form acknowledging the explanation
options.C: Treatment goals, cost per visit, the therapist's training history, and the number of planned sessions
options.D: Diagnosis, the referring physician's opinion, insurance coverage, and research evidence for the treatment

explanation: The correct answer is A (Nature of the treatment, expected benefits, material risks, alternatives, and the right to decline): Informed consent requires the client to understand what the treatment is, what it is expected to achieve, the material risks, the reasonable alternatives including no treatment, and that she may refuse or withdraw. Cost, credentials and insurance details are useful but do not make consent informed about the treatment itself.

question: A 84-year-old woman in a retirement home joins a group exercise class. Before starting, she feels weak after missing breakfast, her pulse is 98 and regular, and her blood pressure seated is 150/84. She asks if she can still do the standing exercises today. What is the best decision?

options.A: Begin the standing exercises now, because her blood pressure is acceptable for a woman her age
options.B: Have her do the standing exercises with a close spotter, because weakness usually passes within minutes
options.C: Begin the class as planned with her seated near the instructor, and reassess after the session
options.D: Offer a snack and fluids, recheck her, and begin with seated exercises while she recovers

explanation: The correct answer is D (Offer a snack and fluids, recheck her, and begin with seated exercises while she recovers): Weakness after skipping breakfast suggests low energy availability, so a snack and fluids come first, followed by a recheck and a lower-risk seated format. A reasonable blood pressure does not explain the weakness, standing with a spotter still carries fall risk, and starting without fuel or a recheck leaves the cause untreated.

question: A physiotherapist orients a new colleague to clinic emergency procedures for fire, medical emergencies and violent clients. The colleague has read the manual and says she is comfortable. Which method best confirms that she can respond in a real emergency?

options.A: Give her a written test on the emergency procedures and accept a passing score as evidence
options.B: Run a simulated medical emergency and observe her response, then hold a debrief
options.C: Ask her to explain the emergency procedures verbally to another staff member during a team meeting
options.D: Have her reread the policy manual carefully and sign a form stating that she understands it

explanation: The correct answer is B (Run a simulated medical emergency and observe her response, then hold a debrief): A simulation lets the physiotherapist see actual performance under pressure and correct gaps in a debrief. Reading, explaining and written tests show knowledge but not the ability to act.

question: At 12 weeks after ACL reconstruction, a physiotherapist wants to assess graft integrity by performing a Lachman test on a 24-year-old man who lies supine and relaxed. The physiotherapist stands beside the affected knee and decides on the starting joint position and hand placement. How should the test be performed?

options.A: Flex the hip and knee to 90 degrees, lift the leg, and push the tibia backward
options.B: Flex the knee to 90 degrees, stabilize the foot, and draw the tibia forward
options.C: Extend the knee fully, apply a valgus force at the ankle, and observe medial gapping
options.D: Flex the knee 20 to 30 degrees, stabilize the femur, and draw the tibia forward

explanation: The correct answer is D (Flex the knee 20 to 30 degrees, stabilize the femur, and draw the tibia forward): The Lachman test is done with the knee in 20 to 30 degrees of flexion, the femur stabilized and the tibia pulled anteriorly to judge translation and end feel. Doing it at 90 degrees describes an anterior drawer, a valgus stress tests the medial collateral ligament, and pushing the tibia backward tests the posterior cruciate ligament.

question: A 19-year-old university hockey player attends physiotherapy for a concussion follow-up. He gives short answers and checks his phone twice during the intake. The physiotherapist wants to build trust before discussing return-to-play. Which opening is most likely to engage him?

options.A: Ask him to rate his symptoms on a checklist and review totals together
options.B: Remind him that his answers help the team and require his full attention
options.C: Ask what he hopes to get back to doing first and listen closely
options.D: Explain the concussion protocol steps and the timeline for return to play

explanation: The correct answer is C (Ask what he hopes to get back to doing first and listen closely): Asking about his own goals shows interest in him as a person and gives him something meaningful to talk about. Explaining the protocol or reviewing a checklist begins with the clinician's agenda, and reminding him to pay attention may feel like a reprimand.

question: A rehabilitation program has a nine-week wait for new outpatient referrals. The waiting clients have stable musculoskeletal conditions. A manager asks the physiotherapist what the program should do for clients while they wait, to keep them informed and safe. Which approach best meets this goal?

options.A: Stay silent until an appointment opens, since an estimate may raise expectations that cannot be met
options.B: Share an estimated wait and a general exercise handout with no further contact until the appointment
options.C: Share an estimated wait, give self-management advice, and explain whom to contact if symptoms worsen
options.D: Phone each client monthly and move anyone reporting increased pain to the front of the list

explanation: The correct answer is C (Share an estimated wait, give self-management advice, and explain whom to contact if symptoms worsen): Waiting clients need an estimated wait, advice they can use meanwhile and clear direction on whom to contact if symptoms worsen. Silence leaves them uninformed, and a handout without a safety net does not support recognition of deterioration. Monthly calls that reorder the list by reported pain are not a fair or reliable triage method.

question: A 31-year-old client with a wrist injury has missed three consecutive appointments and has not replied to two phone messages. Her rehabilitation goals were not yet met at the last visit. The clinic policy requires a plan for closing inactive files. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Phone her twice, then close the file without a letter once attempts are logged
options.B: Send a final letter, document the attempts and discharge reason, and invite her to rebook
options.C: Keep the file open, mailing reminders after each missed visit until she returns
options.D: Call her emergency contact to ask why she stopped attending, then record the answer

explanation: The correct answer is B (Send a final letter, document the attempts and discharge reason, and invite her to rebook): A written closing notice, documented contact attempts, the reason for discharge and an invitation to rebook protect both the client and the clinic. Closing the file after phone calls alone leaves her without formal notice. Keeping a file open with endless reminders delays closure without a plan, and calling an emergency contact about a non-urgent matter breaches her privacy.

question: A physiotherapist needs to examine the hips of a 2-year-old girl at an initial visit. The child cries whenever strangers approach, and her mother is holding her in the treatment room. Which approach is most likely to gain cooperation during the examination?

options.A: Let her play first, then place her alone on the plinth and examine
options.B: Explain the purpose of the assessment in detail to the child before beginning
options.C: Distract her with a tablet video and examine the hips quickly
options.D: Begin with play, keep her on the parent's lap, and examine gently while talking

explanation: The correct answer is D (Begin with play, keep her on the parent's lap, and examine gently while talking): Toddlers need a familiar person nearby and play to lower fear before touch, so cooperation is best gained on the parent's lap with gentle talk. Separating her from her mother after play removes the security she needs. A detailed explanation means little to a 2-year-old, and a screen distraction with a quick examination builds no trust with a child who fears strangers.

question: A 14-year-old gymnast with open growth plates and no pain wants to start a lower limb strength program. Her coach is worried that lifting weights could damage her growth plates and stunt her growth. Which prescription is most appropriate for the physiotherapist to recommend?

options.A: Delay resistance training until growth plates close, because adolescent loading endangers the growth plate
options.B: Bodyweight exercises only until age 18, because external loads are unsafe before skeletal maturity
options.C: Moderate loads for 8 to 15 repetitions with supervised technique, because controlled loading is safe
options.D: Maximal single repetition lifts to build strength, because adolescents respond best to heavy loads

explanation: The correct answer is C (Moderate loads for 8 to 15 repetitions with supervised technique, because controlled loading is safe): Supervised resistance training with moderate loads and good technique is safe and beneficial in skeletally immature athletes, and it does not stunt growth. Waiting for growth plate closure or limiting her to bodyweight work rests on an outdated belief about injury risk. Maximal single repetition lifts add injury risk in a growing athlete and are not needed to build strength.

question: A 44-year-old landscaper has sharp right heel pain after stepping off a ladder. In the corridor he walks with a quick, short stance phase on the right and a longer stance on the left. He winces whenever the right heel loads. Which gait deviation is present?

options.A: Vaulting gait, rising on the stance foot to clear the swinging limb
options.B: Trendelenburg gait, which drops the pelvis when the stance hip abductors fail
options.C: Toe-walking gait, avoiding heel loading by keeping the heel raised in stance
options.D: Antalgic gait, which shortens loading time on the painful limb to reduce pain

explanation: The correct answer is D (Antalgic gait, which shortens loading time on the painful limb to reduce pain): Antalgic gait is a protective pattern in which the person spends as little time as possible loading the painful limb, giving a short stance on that side and a longer stance on the other. Trendelenburg gait is defined by pelvic drop from abductor weakness and vaulting by rising on the stance foot to clear a longer limb. Toe-walking keeps the heel off the ground through stance, whereas this man lands on the heel and winces as it loads.

question: A physiotherapist is about to treat a 7-month-old infant admitted with RSV bronchiolitis. The nurse tells her he is on a standard room with a sign for droplet and contact precautions. Which precautions are appropriate before she enters the room?

options.A: Wear gloves only, since contact with secretions is the only route of transmission in infants
options.B: Perform hand hygiene after leaving only, since the infant is too young to transmit infection
options.C: Perform hand hygiene, then wear a gown, gloves, surgical mask and eye protection
options.D: Wear an N95 respirator and enter a negative pressure room, since the virus spreads by air

explanation: The correct answer is C (Perform hand hygiene, then wear a gown, gloves, surgical mask and eye protection): RSV spreads by droplets and by contact with secretions and surfaces, so droplet and contact precautions apply, with hand hygiene before and after. Airborne precautions are not required, and gloves alone or hand washing only afterwards do not protect against droplet exposure.

question: A 66-year-old woman has bowed legs in standing, tenderness along the medial joint line, and pain when she descends stairs. Squatting is limited by pain. She is otherwise well and takes no regular medication. Which part of the knee is most likely affected by degenerative change?

options.A: The proximal tibiofibular joint, because stair descent loads the fibular head with lateral shear
options.B: The medial tibiofemoral compartment, which takes greater load when the knee is in varus alignment
options.C: The patellofemoral compartment, because stair descent loads the retropatellar surface with high compression
options.D: The lateral tibiofemoral compartment, which carries greater load in bowed-leg standing alignment

explanation: The correct answer is B (The medial tibiofemoral compartment, which takes greater load when the knee is in varus alignment): Varus alignment shifts the load line medially, so the medial tibiofemoral compartment is the most common site of osteoarthritis, and medial joint line tenderness supports it. The lateral compartment is loaded more in valgus alignment. Patellofemoral pain also worsens on stairs, but joint line tenderness and bowed legs point to the medial compartment.

question: The daughter of an 82-year-old man who speaks Tagalog insists on interpreting and asks the physiotherapist not to mention his poor walking prognosis, saying that in their family elders are protected from bad news. A professional interpreter is available by phone. What is the best response?

options.A: Explain that a professional interpreter is needed and he has a right to information
options.B: Share the prognosis with the daughter only and let her decide what he hears
options.C: Respect the family's request, because families in some cultures try to protect elders from distress
options.D: Provide the information in English and note that the daughter can translate afterward

explanation: The correct answer is A (Explain that a professional interpreter is needed and he has a right to information): Clients have a right to information about their own health, and a professional interpreter ensures it is conveyed accurately and neutrally. The physiotherapist can ask him privately how much he wants to know, which respects culture without taking the decision from him. Withholding or filtering information through the daughter does not do this.

question: A 33-year-old badminton player is 12 months after ACL reconstruction. The graph shows her quadriceps strength on the operated side as a percentage of the uninvolved side across the year. She plays in a tournament in three weeks and asks whether she is ready to return to full competition. What is the best advice?

options.A: Allow return at 12 months, since the graft is mature even if quadriceps strength lags behind
options.B: Allow return to singles only, because the strength curve shows the deficit is now steadily shrinking
options.C: Continue progressive strengthening and retest before full competition, because strength is still under 90 percent
options.D: Stop strengthening and begin sport-specific drills, since further strength gains after one year are typically minimal

explanation: The correct answer is C (Continue progressive strengthening and retest before full competition, because strength is still under 90 percent): Her quadriceps strength has risen steadily but remains at 87 percent, below the commonly used 90 percent criterion for returning to pivoting sport. Continued strengthening and retesting is the best plan. A mature graft does not replace muscle strength, and gains can still be made after one year.

question: A physiotherapist assesses a 48-year-old man who weighs 115 kg and has a spinal cord injury with no lower limb movement. He needs a bed-to-chair transfer, and a student suggests that two staff lift him manually. Which principle best guides the decision about equipment?

options.A: Two staff can lift him manually if both bend their knees and count together before lifting
options.B: A gait belt makes a two-person manual lift acceptable, because it distributes the lifting load evenly
options.C: Use a mechanical lift, since risk assessment shows dependent clients should not be lifted manually
options.D: A transfer board with one trained staff member is enough, since sliding the client avoids lifting

explanation: The correct answer is C (Use a mechanical lift, since risk assessment shows dependent clients should not be lifted manually): A client who cannot assist is a high-risk transfer, and a risk assessment supports a mechanical lift rather than manual lifting by staff. Good technique does not remove the injury risk to staff or the client, and a gait belt is for guiding an assisting client rather than lifting a dependent one.

question: A 22-year-old man at Rancho level IV, two weeks after a severe brain injury, is shouting and trying to leave the unit during a mobility session in a bright, busy gym. He is not violent but cannot attend to instructions. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Use a variety of group activities with music to hold his attention on the task
options.B: Correct his confused statements firmly and orient him to date, place and injury repeatedly
options.C: Continue the planned gait training with firm repeated commands to improve his attention
options.D: Reduce stimulation, use a quiet room with a calm tone and keep demands short and simple

explanation: The correct answer is D (Reduce stimulation, use a quiet room with a calm tone and keep demands short and simple): At the agitated stage the nervous system is easily overloaded, so low stimulation, calm communication and brief simple tasks reduce agitation. Repeated correction and orientation drills increase frustration. Busy group settings and firm commands add stimulation and worsen behaviour.

question: A 66-year-old postmenopausal woman brings a bone density report to her physiotherapy visit and asks what it means. Her T-scores are shown in the table. She has never had a fracture. Using the World Health Organization categories, how should the physiotherapist describe her bone status?

options.A: Osteoporosis, because the lowest site T-score is below minus 2.5 at the lumbar spine
options.B: Normal bone density, because Z-scores are above minus 2.0 at all three sites
options.C: Osteopenia, because both hip T-scores lie between minus 1.0 and minus 2.5
options.D: Osteopenia, because the average of the three T-scores falls between minus 1.0 and minus 2.5

image_params.title: Bone mineral density report
image_params.caption: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry results

explanation: The correct answer is A (Osteoporosis, because the lowest site T-score is below minus 2.5 at the lumbar spine): The WHO classification uses the lowest T-score from a measured site, and a lumbar spine T-score of minus 2.7 is below minus 2.5, which defines osteoporosis. Averaging sites is not used, and Z-scores compare with age-matched peers rather than defining bone status. Hip scores in the osteopenic range do not override the lumbar result.

question: A physiotherapist completes an observation checklist for an assistant performing a stand-pivot transfer with a client on a hospital ward. Clinic policy requires every safety item to be done correctly before independent assignment. The table shows the findings. Which conclusion is appropriate?

options.A: Competence cannot be judged, because one observation gives too little information to decide
options.B: Competence is confirmed because five of six items were done, and footwear can be taught later
options.C: Competence is not yet confirmed, so give feedback and observe the transfer again before assigning it
options.D: Competence is confirmed for stable clients only, because the missed item matters mainly for unstable clients

image_params.title: Observation checklist: stand-pivot transfer
image_params.caption: Single observation on one ward.

explanation: The correct answer is C (Competence is not yet confirmed, so give feedback and observe the transfer again before assigning it): Policy requires every safety item, and footwear was not checked, so the task is not ready for independent assignment. The right step is feedback and a repeat observation. Accepting five of six or limiting by client type ignores the standard that was set.

question: A 59-year-old man is two weeks after hip arthroplasty. During gait training he reports sudden sharp chest pain on inspiration and breathlessness. His heart rate is 118 beats per minute and oxygen saturation is 90 percent on room air. What should the physiotherapist do first?

options.A: Return him to bed and recheck vital signs in ten minutes before informing the nurse
options.B: Apply a heat pack to the chest wall and have him do deep breathing exercises standing
options.C: Continue gait at a slower pace with pursed-lip breathing, since exertional dyspnea is expected after surgery
options.D: Stop activity, help him sit, and call for urgent medical help, as pulmonary embolism is suspected

explanation: The correct answer is D (Stop activity, help him sit, and call for urgent medical help, as pulmonary embolism is suspected): Sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia and low oxygen saturation soon after orthopedic surgery suggest pulmonary embolism. The immediate priority is to stop activity, keep him safe and summon emergency help. Delay, continued exertion or local treatment do not address a life-threatening condition.

question: A 39-year-old violinist has an ache 4 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, over the supinator muscle mass, aggravated by resisted forearm supination and resisted middle finger extension but not by resisted wrist extension. The epicondyle itself is not tender, and grip strength is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Pronator teres syndrome, because repetitive forearm pronation under load compresses the median nerve proximally
options.B: Radial tunnel syndrome, because pain over the supinator with resisted supination implicates the posterior interosseous nerve
options.C: Cervical radiculopathy at C6, because lateral forearm pain with muscle ache frequently refers from the neck
options.D: Lateral epicondylalgia, because pain near the common extensor origin is typical of tendon overload in musicians

explanation: The correct answer is B (Radial tunnel syndrome, because pain over the supinator with resisted supination implicates the posterior interosseous nerve): Tenderness over the supinator, pain with resisted supination and middle finger extension, and painless resisted wrist extension at a normal epicondyle suggest radial tunnel syndrome. Lateral epicondylalgia would be tender at the epicondyle with pain on resisted wrist extension, and median nerve compression would involve the volar forearm.

question: An 80-year-old man with Parkinson disease reports dizziness on standing. In clinic his blood pressure is 140 over 84 lying and 108 over 64 after three minutes of standing, and he feels faint. He is scheduled for standing balance exercises today. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Return him to sitting, hold standing exercises, teach slow position changes, and inform his physician
options.B: Seat him until symptoms settle, then resume standing exercises with the physiotherapist close by
options.C: Switch to seated and supine exercises today and report the readings in his chart
options.D: Apply compression stockings and an abdominal binder, then continue standing exercises with close supervision

explanation: The correct answer is A (Return him to sitting, hold standing exercises, teach slow position changes, and inform his physician): A systolic drop of 32 mmHg with faintness on standing is orthostatic hypotension, so standing exercises are unsafe until it is assessed, and his physician must know because Parkinson medication can contribute. Teaching slow position changes reduces his risk in daily life. Resuming standing work after a rest or with supports still exposes him to syncope, and charting the readings alone leaves the prescriber uninformed.

question: A 35-year-old soccer player felt a tearing in his calf during a sprint. Two days later he has extensive bruising, a palpable gap in the medial calf at the musculotendinous junction, and cannot rise onto the toes of that leg. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start massage to the gap to disperse hematoma, because early massage speeds healing
options.B: Begin eccentric calf loading from tomorrow, because early loading restores strength after any strain
options.C: Treat as a grade I strain with compression and walking, because gaps follow bleeding
options.D: Refer to an orthopedic surgeon for imaging, because a complete gastrocnemius tear is suspected

explanation: The correct answer is D (Refer to an orthopedic surgeon for imaging, because a complete gastrocnemius tear is suspected): A palpable defect with extensive bruising and loss of function indicates a grade III tear, and imaging and surgical opinion are appropriate. Loading or massage over an acute complete tear can worsen bleeding and separation, and a grade I strain would not produce a gap.

question: A 3-year-old will not walk or sit up, cries when picked up, and has a low-grade fever. Hip range of motion is full and painless, but he resists forward bending of the spine. Back percussion is tender. Which condition is most likely?

options.A: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, an avascular necrosis causing a painless limp and restricted abduction
options.B: Transient synovitis of the hip, an irritable joint causing limp and pain with hip rotation
options.C: Discitis, infection of the intervertebral disc space, presenting with refusal to walk or sit
options.D: Septic arthritis of the hip, a joint infection causing severe pain with any hip movement

explanation: The correct answer is C (Discitis, infection of the intervertebral disc space, presenting with refusal to walk or sit): A young child with refusal to walk or sit, spinal stiffness, back tenderness and low-grade fever fits discitis. The full, painless hip motion argues against hip causes such as synovitis or septic arthritis, and Perthes disease is a painless limp with restricted hip motion. MRI and blood tests confirm discitis.

question: A 66-year-old retired man reports clumsy hands, difficulty with buttons, and a wide-based unsteady gait over six months. He has mild neck stiffness. The physiotherapist finds a positive Hoffmann sign bilaterally and brisk knee reflexes. Which interpretation and action are most appropriate?

options.A: Suspect age-related change and prescribe balance training, because gait change and stiffness are common with age
options.B: Suspect carpal tunnel syndrome and splint both wrists, because hand clumsiness is typical of that condition
options.C: Suspect cervical radiculopathy and begin traction, because brisk reflexes and arm symptoms indicate root irritation
options.D: Suspect cervical myelopathy and refer for medical assessment, because upper motor neuron signs indicate cord compression

explanation: The correct answer is D (Suspect cervical myelopathy and refer for medical assessment, because upper motor neuron signs indicate cord compression): Hand clumsiness, gait disturbance, a positive Hoffmann sign and hyperreflexia are upper motor neuron signs of degenerative cervical myelopathy. Referral for medical assessment is needed because cord compression can progress. Radiculopathy produces lower motor neuron findings, and carpal tunnel does not cause hyperreflexia or gait change.

question: A 34-year-old woman has unilateral buttock pain. The physiotherapist performs five sacroiliac provocation tests in a standard order with the client relaxed. Four are positive, and repeated active lumbar movements, including repeated extension, do not change her symptoms. How should these results be interpreted for the likely source of her pain?

options.A: Positive tests implicate the joint only if all five are positive
options.B: Pain is lumbar in origin since repeated extension left symptoms unchanged
options.C: Tests also stress the hip, so a hip source is likelier
options.D: Four positive tests with no lumbar response make a sacroiliac source likely

cluster_text: A 33-year-old woman, five months postpartum, reports right buttock pain when rolling in bed and standing on one leg. Pain stays above the knee. Lumbar movements and repeated extension do not change her symptoms. Distraction, thigh thrust, sacral thrust and Gaenslen tests reproduce her familiar pain, but compression does not. Hip internal rotation is full and painless.
explanation: The correct answer is D (Four positive tests with no lumbar response make a sacroiliac source likely): A cluster of three or more positive provocation tests with no lumbar response supports a sacroiliac source. Requiring all five tests to be positive ignores how the cluster is interpreted. No change with repeated extension does not prove a lumbar origin, and nothing in her findings points to the hip.

question: The physiotherapist considers whether the hip joint, rather than the sacroiliac joint, could be the primary source of the client's pain, and examines the hip in supine and standing as part of a differential assessment. Which finding in this case argues most strongly against hip joint pathology as the primary source of her pain?

options.A: Buttock pain, since hip joint disease usually produces groin pain alone
options.B: Full, painless hip internal rotation, since hip joint disease usually limits and provokes rotation
options.C: Pain when rolling in bed, since hip conditions mainly hurt in upright standing
options.D: Pain with single-leg stance, since hip joint pain seldom changes with loading

cluster_text: A 33-year-old woman, five months postpartum, reports right buttock pain when rolling in bed and standing on one leg. Pain stays above the knee. Lumbar movements and repeated extension do not change her symptoms. Distraction, thigh thrust, sacral thrust and Gaenslen tests reproduce her familiar pain, but compression does not. Hip internal rotation is full and painless.
explanation: The correct answer is B (Full, painless hip internal rotation, since hip joint disease usually limits and provokes rotation): Hip joint disease typically reduces and provokes internal rotation, so full painless rotation argues against it as the main source. Hip pain can be felt in the buttock as well as the groin, often increases with single-leg stance, and may be provoked by bed mobility, so those findings do not separate hip from sacroiliac pain.

question: At a follow-up visit two weeks after the start of her home exercise program, the woman reports several new symptoms. Her vital signs are normal and she is taking no new medications. The physiotherapist must decide which of them needs the most urgent medical referral. Which symptom is it?

options.A: Pain waking her once when she rolls onto her right side, because it suggests infection
options.B: New saddle numbness with difficulty starting urination, because it suggests cauda equina compression
options.C: Intermittent tingling in the lateral calf when sitting, because it suggests lumbar root irritation
options.D: Mild morning stiffness lasting twenty minutes, because it suggests an inflammatory arthritis

cluster_text: A 33-year-old woman, five months postpartum, reports right buttock pain when rolling in bed and standing on one leg. Pain stays above the knee. Lumbar movements and repeated extension do not change her symptoms. Distraction, thigh thrust, sacral thrust and Gaenslen tests reproduce her familiar pain, but compression does not. Hip internal rotation is full and painless.
explanation: The correct answer is B (New saddle numbness with difficulty starting urination, because it suggests cauda equina compression): Saddle numbness with bladder difficulty are cauda equina warning signs and need emergency assessment. Intermittent root-type symptoms, brief positional night waking, and short morning stiffness warrant monitoring or routine follow-up but not an urgent referral.

question: A 72-year-old woman from a First Nations community is hospitalized after a fall. She explains that important decisions are made together with her daughters and a community Elder, and asks that they join rehabilitation planning. She is capable of consenting. How should the physiotherapist proceed?

options.A: Include her family and Elder, then share her full chart so everyone is informed
options.B: Meet her alone first for every decision, then relay the plan to her family
options.C: Include the daughters and Elder, and have them agree on the plan for her
options.D: Include the people she names in planning meetings, confirm her consent, and use plain language

explanation: The correct answer is D (Include the people she names in planning meetings, confirm her consent, and use plain language): A capable client may choose who takes part in her care decisions, and culturally safe practice respects that while her consent still governs what is shared. Sharing her full chart goes beyond what she agreed to. Meeting her alone overrides her stated preference for group decisions, and letting relatives agree on the plan for her removes her own authority.

question: A 12-year-old girl was found to have a curve of 18 degrees at age 11. She is Risser grade 1 and premenarchal. The chart plots her Cobb angles at each follow-up radiograph. Which interpretation of the trend is most appropriate?

options.A: Curve progression well above radiographic measurement error, so orthopedic referral is warranted
options.B: Variation within the usual radiographic measurement error, so continue observation at the same interval
options.C: Improvement from the postural exercise program, so the present program should continue unchanged
options.D: Expected growth-related change that levels off before skeletal maturity, so no referral is needed

image_params.title: Cobb angle at each radiograph
image_params.caption: Standing posteroanterior radiographs measured by the same observer

explanation: The correct answer is A (Curve progression well above radiographic measurement error, so orthopedic referral is warranted): A rise from 18 to 31 degrees over 18 months in a skeletally immature girl is far above the roughly 5 degree measurement error and is clear progression. At Risser 1 with growth remaining, the risk of further progression is high, so orthopedic assessment for bracing or surgery is needed. The trend shows worsening, not stability or improvement.

question: The orders for a 79-year-old man after cemented hip hemiarthroplasty for a femoral neck fracture state toe-touch weight bearing on the left leg. His daughter asks the physiotherapist what this means when he walks with a walker. Which description is correct?

options.A: Full body weight may go through the leg whenever a walker is used for support
options.B: The foot may rest lightly on the floor for balance, with minimal load
options.C: Up to half of body weight may go through the leg during each step
options.D: About one quarter of body weight may go through the leg, measured on a bathroom scale

explanation: The correct answer is B (The foot may rest lightly on the floor for balance, with minimal load): Toe-touch weight bearing means the toes contact the floor for balance only, with almost no load through the limb. Half of body weight corresponds to partial weight bearing, about one quarter is a smaller partial prescription, and a walker does not convert the status into full weight bearing.

question: A 35-year-old woman asks for a pelvic floor assessment and says she was assaulted several years ago. She becomes quiet as the physiotherapist explains an internal examination. Her previous physician notes show a normal examination. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Proceed with the internal examination, because the previous normal result shows she tolerated it before
options.B: Cancel treatment and refer her for counselling, because her history makes physiotherapy unsuitable for her
options.C: Continue the explanation without comment, because stopping would reinforce her anxiety about the examination
options.D: Pause, acknowledge her reaction, and offer a different approach or deferral of the internal part

explanation: The correct answer is D (Pause, acknowledge her reaction, and offer a different approach or deferral of the internal part): Trauma-informed care means noticing signs of distress, giving control back and offering alternatives or delay. A past tolerated exam does not guarantee current consent, and discharging her or ignoring her silence ignores her needs and autonomy.

question: A physiotherapist completes an insurer progress report for a client with a knee fracture, and the table shows the outcome measures. The minimal clinically important difference for the Lower Extremity Functional Scale is 9 points. Which statement accurately reflects the table?

options.A: The LEFS rose 18 points, exceeding the minimal clinically important difference of 9
options.B: Pain improved by 5 points, a larger change than the LEFS improvement
options.C: The LEFS rose 9 points, which equals the minimal clinically important difference
options.D: The LEFS improved by 52 points, exceeding the minimal clinically important difference

image_params.title: Outcome measures
image_params.caption: Right tibial plateau fracture, non-operative management.

explanation: The correct answer is A (The LEFS rose 18 points, exceeding the minimal clinically important difference of 9): The LEFS rose from 34 to 52, a change of 18 points, which is larger than the minimal clinically important difference of 9. A score of 52 is the final value, not the change. A 9 point rise misreads the table, and pain improved by only 3 points, which does not exceed the LEFS change.

question: A newly graduated physiotherapist wants useful feedback from her mentor on her manual therapy skills after three months in practice. She is unsure how to ask so that the feedback will be specific and usable. Which request is most likely to produce specific, helpful feedback?

options.A: Ask the mentor to observe one treatment and comment on her hand placement and positioning
options.B: Ask the mentor to provide a numerical rating of her professional skills on a ten-point scale
options.C: Ask the mentor whether she is performing satisfactorily overall as a newly graduated clinician this year
options.D: Ask the mentor to review all her treatment notes every month and approve them for accuracy

explanation: The correct answer is A (Ask the mentor to observe one treatment and comment on her hand placement and positioning): A focused request tied to an observed performance and named skills gives the mentor something concrete to comment on. General questions about overall performance, note review, or a numerical rating are vague and do not give guidance on what to change in the technique.

question: An 81-year-old woman lives alone. She needs help with finances, transportation and heavy housework, but bathes, dresses and prepares simple meals independently, and walks with a cane at a slow pace. Using the Clinical Frailty Scale, which rating best describes her?

options.A: Level 6, moderately frail, because she needs regular help with all outside activities and housekeeping
options.B: Level 5, mildly frail, because she needs help with higher-order tasks such as finances and transport
options.C: Level 3, managing well, because she completes all her basic activities of daily living independently
options.D: Level 4, vulnerable, because she is not dependent but slowing and symptoms limit her activities

explanation: The correct answer is B (Level 5, mildly frail, because she needs help with higher-order tasks such as finances and transport): On the Clinical Frailty Scale, level 5 describes people who need help with higher-order instrumental activities such as finances, transport and heavy housework while remaining independent in personal care. Level 6 needs help with all outside activities and some personal care, and levels 3 and 4 involve fewer limits.

question: A physiotherapist plans to screen a 45-year-old client with chronic pain for abuse in a private room. The client has been seen three times, attends alone, and has not disclosed any concerns. The physiotherapist wants an opening that is non-accusatory and builds trust. Which opening is best?

options.A: Has your husband ever hit you or forced you to do anything?
options.B: Because abuse can affect health, I ask all clients: do you feel safe at home?
options.C: Your pain pattern is common in abuse, so is someone hurting you at home?
options.D: I have to ask this question of everyone, so please just answer yes or no

explanation: The correct answer is B (Because abuse can affect health, I ask all clients: do you feel safe at home?): Explaining why the question is asked and that it is routine reduces stigma and invites an honest reply. Linking her pain to abuse can feel like an accusation. A rushed yes or no request discourages disclosure, and assuming a husband makes assumptions about her relationship and sexuality.

question: A 25-year-old man is brought to hospital after a motorcycle collision. He opens his eyes only to painful stimulation, speaks in confused sentences, and moves his hand toward the source of a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score and injury classification?

options.A: 11, a moderate injury, from eye 2, verbal 4 and motor 5
options.B: 10, a moderate injury, from eye 2, verbal 3 and motor 5
options.C: 8, a severe injury, from eye 2, verbal 2 and motor 4
options.D: 13, a mild injury, from eye 3, verbal 4 and motor 6

explanation: The correct answer is A (11, a moderate injury, from eye 2, verbal 4 and motor 5): Eye opening to pain scores 2, confused conversation scores 4, and localizing to pain scores 5, giving 11, which falls in the moderate range of 9 to 12. The other totals come from scoring one component too low or too high, and mild injury is 13 to 15 while severe is 8 or below.

question: A 58-year-old man taking a high-dose statin joined a boot-camp class last week. Today he reports diffuse muscle pain, marked weakness and tea-coloured urine, and he wants to finish today's session. His vital signs are normal. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Stop exercise and arrange same-day medical assessment with creatine kinase testing, because rhabdomyolysis is possible
options.B: Advise two days of rest and return if dark urine persists, because urine colour reflects hydration
options.C: Allow reduced-intensity exercise and increase water intake, because mild dehydration explains the dark urine and soreness
options.D: Treat as delayed onset muscle soreness with gentle stretching and ice, because pain follows new exercise

explanation: The correct answer is A (Stop exercise and arrange same-day medical assessment with creatine kinase testing, because rhabdomyolysis is possible): A statin, new strenuous exercise, weakness and dark urine are warning signs of rhabdomyolysis, which can injure the kidneys and requires prompt medical testing and treatment. Exercise, simple hydration advice, or waiting would delay care.

question: A 63-year-old woman learns four exercises after rotator cuff repair. When asked if she understands, she nods and says everything is clear. Her husband quietly mentions that she often agrees to avoid delaying the session. How should the physiotherapist confirm that she can perform the program safely at home?

options.A: Have her demonstrate the hardest exercise and give a printed sheet for the others
options.B: Ask her to demonstrate each exercise and explain it back, then correct errors and re-check
options.C: Ask if she has questions and give her a printed sheet with the details
options.D: Teach her husband the exercises as well so he can prompt her at home

explanation: The correct answer is B (Ask her to demonstrate each exercise and explain it back, then correct errors and re-check): Teach-back and return demonstration show whether she can actually perform each exercise, which a nod does not, especially when her husband says she agrees to avoid delay. Correcting errors and re-checking closes the loop. Checking only the hardest exercise leaves the others unverified, and asking for questions or handing out a sheet relies on her saying she understands. Involving her husband helps support but does not confirm her own ability.

question: A physiotherapy student on placement asks a 77-year-old patient with moderate dementia for consent to begin treatment. The patient says yes, then a minute later seems confused about what she agreed to. The student looks to her supervisor for guidance. What should the supervisor guide the student to do?

options.A: Proceed with treatment because she verbally agreed, and document that agreement carefully in the clinical chart
options.B: Postpone all treatment until a physician formally declares her incapable of consenting to her physiotherapy care
options.C: Check her understanding of the treatment, and if capacity is doubtful, ask the legal substitute decision-maker
options.D: Ask any visiting relative to sign the consent form without checking who the legal substitute is

explanation: The correct answer is C (Check her understanding of the treatment, and if capacity is doubtful, ask the legal substitute decision-maker): Capacity is specific to the decision and must be assessed by checking understanding of the treatment, its purpose and risks. If she cannot, the person identified in provincial law as substitute decision-maker decides. A hasty verbal yes, waiting for a formal declaration, or consent from any relative does not meet the legal standard.

question: A 49-year-old man has left calf pain for two days after a long-haul flight. He has tenderness along the deep veins, but no leg swelling, no pitting edema and only 1 centimetre of calf asymmetry. He has no cancer, surgery or prior clots, and muscle strain is as likely. What is his Wells score?

options.A: Minus 1, so DVT is unlikely and a D-dimer test is the usual next step
options.B: Zero, so DVT is unlikely and no further testing is needed before exercise
options.C: Plus 1, so DVT is unlikely and a D-dimer test is the usual next step
options.D: Plus 2, so DVT is likely and ultrasound imaging is the usual next step

explanation: The correct answer is A (Minus 1, so DVT is unlikely and a D-dimer test is the usual next step): Localized tenderness along the deep veins adds one point, and because a muscle strain is as likely as DVT two points are subtracted, giving a score of minus 1. A score below 2 means DVT is unlikely in the two-level Wells model, and a D-dimer test is usually the next step. Ignoring the alternative-diagnosis item produces a score of plus 1.

question: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson disease, Hoehn and Yahr stage 2, stands in clinic with a stooped posture: rounded upper back, head forward and mildly bent hips and knees. He walks independently and has mild rigidity but no postural instability. Which exercise emphasis best addresses this posture?

options.A: Pectoral and hip flexor strengthening against resistance, to improve upper body power for transfers
options.B: Back and hip extensor strengthening with thoracic extension mobility and wall-based postural cueing
options.C: Static stretching of the back extensors held for sixty seconds, to relieve rigidity in the spine
options.D: Abdominal flexion strengthening with forward trunk curls to improve core control and trunk stability

explanation: The correct answer is B (Back and hip extensor strengthening with thoracic extension mobility and wall-based postural cueing): The stooped, flexed posture of Parkinson disease is addressed by strengthening the extensors that are lengthened and weak, mobilizing the stiff thoracic spine and cueing upright alignment against a wall. Strengthening the flexors or pectorals deepens the flexed pattern, and stretching the extensors targets muscles that are already lengthened.

question: A 34-year-old paramedic had a tibial shaft fracture fixed with an intramedullary nail. The surgeon ordered partial weight-bearing at 50 percent of body weight, and he weighs 80 kg. He practises loading the leg on a bathroom scale with crutches. The table shows five trials. What should the physiotherapist do next?

options.A: Accept his loading as safe for gait, because most trials stayed within the prescribed limit
options.B: Progress to full weight-bearing, because his average reading is close to the prescribed limit
options.C: Change the order to non-weight-bearing for safety, because two trials exceeded the prescribed limit
options.D: Repeat scale practice with visual feedback until readings stay under the limit, then progress gait

image_params.title: Single-leg scale loading practice
image_params.caption: Client body weight is 80 kg.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Repeat scale practice with visual feedback until readings stay under the limit, then progress gait): Trials 3 and 5 reached 63 and 66 kg, well above the 40 kg limit, so he cannot yet judge his load reliably and needs more feedback training. Relying on an average or on most trials ignores the overloads. Changing the weight-bearing order is the surgeon's decision, not the physiotherapist's.

question: A physiotherapist is paid per visit at a clinic. A client with chronic low back pain has plateaued after twelve visits, and the physiotherapist believes a pain science education program with fewer visits would help more. What is the best approach?

options.A: Reduce visits only if the client asks, to avoid disrupting the established routine
options.B: Change the plan for client benefit and explain why, even though it lowers her income
options.C: Keep the schedule and add a home program, since plateaus often pass with time
options.D: Ask the clinic owner to approve the plan change before offering it to her

explanation: The correct answer is B (Change the plan for client benefit and explain why, even though it lowers her income): Care decisions must rest on what benefits the client, not on how the physiotherapist is paid, so the plan is changed and the reason explained openly. Waiting for the client to ask passes professional judgment to her. Keeping the schedule after a plateau serves income more than outcome, and owner approval is not needed to offer a better clinical plan.

question: A physiotherapist plans a first exercise session for a 6-year-old girl with a myelomeningocele who has had several surgeries and bladder catheterizations. The clinic stocks resistance bands, therapy balls and examination gloves of several materials. What precaution is most important about equipment?

options.A: Use latex equipment with a barrier layer, because skin contact is the only route of exposure
options.B: Use powder-free latex gloves with standard bands, because removing the powder prevents latex sensitization
options.C: Use latex-free bands, balls and gloves, because repeated exposure raises her risk of latex allergy
options.D: Use latex equipment after a negative patch test, because it confirms she is not allergic

explanation: The correct answer is C (Use latex-free bands, balls and gloves, because repeated exposure raises her risk of latex allergy): Children with spina bifida are at high risk of latex allergy because of repeated surgical and catheter exposure, so all contact items should be latex-free. Powder-free gloves still contain latex proteins, a negative patch test does not rule out allergy, and latex proteins can also reach the airway and mucosa, not just skin.

question: A physiotherapist is repeatedly belittled in front of patients by a senior colleague. A private request to stop was ignored, and she worries about the effect on her references. The workplace has a written harassment policy and a human resources office. What should she do next?

options.A: Document each incident with dates and witnesses, then report through the harassment policy to human resources
options.B: Confront the colleague publicly during the next departmental meeting so that colleagues can observe the pattern
options.C: Continue making private requests for another month, giving the senior colleague a reasonable opportunity to change
options.D: Request a transfer to a different clinic location and say nothing about the reason to management

explanation: The correct answer is A (Document each incident with dates and witnesses, then report through the harassment policy to human resources): A private request has already failed, so the next step is to use the formal process with careful documentation. Public confrontation escalates conflict, a silent transfer leaves the problem for others, and further delay allows the behaviour to continue.

question: A 71-year-old woman is describing a fall at home. The physiotherapist, short on time, has already interrupted her twice, and the client now says 'never mind, it was nothing.' She folds her arms and looks toward the door. What should the physiotherapist do to repair rapport?

options.A: Apologize for interrupting and invite her to tell the story her way
options.B: Tell her that the details matter for safety and ask her to continue
options.C: Continue with the standard falls screening questions to cover the essential items efficiently
options.D: Thank her for sharing and move on to the physical examination at once

explanation: The correct answer is A (Apologize for interrupting and invite her to tell the story her way): A brief apology owns the mistake and an open invitation gives control of the story back to her, which restores trust. Pressing on with screening, stressing safety or moving to the examination all ignore that she has withdrawn because she felt unheard.

question: A 20-year-old cyclist is admitted after a high-energy tibial fracture and surgical fixation. A physiotherapist is asked to teach the nursing staff which early sign best suggests developing acute compartment syndrome in the leg. Which sign should be identified first?

options.A: Pallor of the foot, because skin colour changes first when pressure rises in the compartment
options.B: Paralysis of the toes, because motor loss is the earliest sign of nerve compromise
options.C: Pain out of proportion to injury and worsened by passive stretch, because nerves become ischemic
options.D: Absent dorsalis pedis pulse, because arterial flow stops early as compartment pressure rises

explanation: The correct answer is C (Pain out of proportion to injury and worsened by passive stretch, because nerves become ischemic): Pain that is disproportionate and increases with passive stretch is the earliest and most reliable sign of acute compartment syndrome. Pulse loss, pallor, and paralysis are late findings, because arterial inflow is usually preserved until pressures are very high.

question: A 71-year-old man, two weeks after a right hemisphere stroke, sits at the edge of the bed pushing strongly toward his weak left side, and resists when his trunk is moved toward midline. He believes he is upright when tilted and feels unwell when corrected. How should the physiotherapist retrain his posture?

options.A: Passively push his trunk to midline with firm manual force, repeating until the pushing reduces
options.B: Prop him with pillows on the left side so the push cannot move him sideways
options.C: Give visual feedback with a mirror or vertical frame, and practise active weight shift to midline
options.D: Have him practise sitting with his eyes closed, relying on trunk sensation to find midline

explanation: The correct answer is C (Give visual feedback with a mirror or vertical frame, and practise active weight shift to midline): In pusher behaviour the perception of vertical is altered, so retraining uses intact vision to show where upright is, followed by active movement toward midline. Forced manual correction meets resistance and distress, and propping offers passive support without learning. Removing vision asks him to rely on the very sense that is distorted.

question: A 62-year-old woman with paraplegia has a stage 2 pressure injury over her left greater trochanter and uses a pressure-redistributing mattress. Staff have been placing her in 90-degree left side-lying overnight. The physiotherapist updates the positioning plan. Which turning position is most appropriate overnight?

options.A: Place a ring cushion under the left hip, because it relieves pressure over the injured trochanter
options.B: Position supine with the head of bed raised to 60 degrees overnight to protect the trochanter
options.C: Alternate full 90-degree right and left side-lying every two hours, because the mattress redistributes pressure
options.D: Use 30-degree tilts supported by pillows, alternating sides so the injured trochanter bears no direct load

explanation: The correct answer is D (Use 30-degree tilts supported by pillows, alternating sides so the injured trochanter bears no direct load): A 30-degree tilt places weight on the fleshy buttock rather than the trochanter and keeps pressure off the injured site. Full 90-degree lying on the injured side loads the trochanter directly, a steep head-up angle adds sacral shear, and ring cushions create a pressure ridge.

question: A 4-year-old boy has a limp for two days after a cold. He is afebrile, bears weight with a limp, and has mild pain at the extremes of hip rotation. ESR is 12 mm/h and white count is 8.5 ×10⁹/L. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, supported by the limp, mild restriction of hip rotation and the child's age
options.B: Septic arthritis, supported by the recent cold, the limp and pain at end-range hip rotation
options.C: Transient synovitis, supported by the afebrile state, weight bearing and normal inflammatory markers
options.D: Osteomyelitis of the femoral neck, supported by the limp, recent illness and pain with hip movement

explanation: The correct answer is C (Transient synovitis, supported by the afebrile state, weight bearing and normal inflammatory markers): A limp after a viral illness in an afebrile child who can bear weight, with normal inflammatory markers, favours transient synovitis, which resolves within a week or two. Septic arthritis would bring fever, refusal to bear weight and raised markers. Perthes disease develops over weeks to months, and osteomyelitis brings fever and focal bone tenderness.

question: A private clinic wants to introduce a fee for appointments cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. The owner asks the physiotherapist when clients must be told about this policy for the fee to be fair and enforceable. When should clients be informed?

options.A: Through a sign in the waiting room, which is enough notice for all clients attending
options.B: When the first late cancellation happens, so the fee can be explained as the situation arises
options.C: At or before the first visit, in writing, so the client agrees to the policy beforehand
options.D: On the first invoice that includes the fee, so the client sees the exact amount owing

explanation: The correct answer is C (At or before the first visit, in writing, so the client agrees to the policy beforehand): Clients can only consent to a charge they know about, so the policy should be explained and agreed to, preferably in writing, before it can apply. Telling them after the event, relying on a posted sign, or revealing it on an invoice does not give a chance to agree beforehand.

question: An adult client's final physiotherapy entry was dated 12 June 2018, and the clinic retains adult records for ten years from the last entry under the college standard. The clinic is clearing its archive and wants the earliest permitted destruction date for this record. Which date is correct?

options.A: 12 June 2026, because eight years covers the usual limitation period for claims
options.B: 12 June 2028, because retention runs ten years from the final documented entry
options.C: 12 June 2025, because seven years matches the usual business records period
options.D: 12 June 2033, because the clock restarts when the client's file is archived

explanation: The correct answer is B (12 June 2028, because retention runs ten years from the final documented entry): Ten years added to 12 June 2018 gives 12 June 2028 as the earliest date the record may be destroyed. The business-records and claims periods do not set the clinical retention rule, and archiving a file does not restart the clock. A later date would be permissible but is not the earliest.

question: A 17-year-old is six months after ACL reconstruction and asks about return to sport. The single-leg hop for distance measures 128 cm on the involved leg and 160 cm on the uninvolved leg. The clinic uses a limb symmetry index of at least 90 percent as one criterion. What is the index?

options.A: 20 percent, which falls well below the clinic criterion of 90 percent
options.B: 25 percent, which falls well below the clinic criterion of 90 percent
options.C: 125 percent, which exceeds the clinic criterion of 90 percent
options.D: 80 percent, which falls below the clinic criterion of 90 percent

explanation: The correct answer is D (80 percent, which falls below the clinic criterion of 90 percent): The index divides the involved limb by the uninvolved limb: 128 divided by 160 equals 0.80, or 80 percent. Dividing the other way gives 125, and subtracting yields a deficit of 20 percent or, relative to the involved limb, 25 percent. Eighty percent does not meet the criterion, so return to sport should wait.
