image_params.caption: Scores recorded by the assistant.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Reassess the client in person and revise the plan, because pain exceeded the trigger repeatedly): Pain scores have crossed the trigger in the plan for several sessions, which should have prompted contact and now requires reassessment. Changing volume or adding a modality through the assistant substitutes for a clinical decision, and waiting delays care.

question: A 62 year old man joins a community exercise program. At screening his resting blood pressure is 182/108 on two measures five minutes apart. He feels well, takes no medication and has never had his blood pressure checked. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Start light walking and recheck after the session, since he feels well and has no symptoms
options.B: Defer exercise and refer him for prompt medical assessment, since resting pressure is too high
options.C: Advise him to cut salt for one month and retest before starting exercise
options.D: Allow low intensity exercise with pressure checks every ten minutes, since monitoring makes it safe

explanation: The correct answer is B (Defer exercise and refer him for prompt medical assessment, since resting pressure is too high): A resting pressure of 182/108 confirmed on two measures is high enough that exercise should be deferred until a physician evaluates him, even if he has no symptoms. A month of salt reduction delays needed assessment, and monitoring during exercise does not make unassessed severe hypertension safe.

question: A physiotherapist at a low-income community clinic prescribes resistance band exercises for a 55-year-old woman with rotator cuff tendinopathy. The woman says she cannot afford bands because her food budget is already tight this month. Which response best addresses this social barrier to her rehabilitation?

options.A: Teach equivalent exercises with household items and share community programs, because cost should not limit participation
options.B: Recommend that she reduce other household spending to buy bands, because equipment is essential to treatment
options.C: Lend her clinic bands without discussing her circumstances, because individual favours resolve systemic inequity for clients
options.D: Delay the strengthening phase until she can buy bands, because specific equipment ensures correct tendon loading

explanation: The correct answer is A (Teach equivalent exercises with household items and share community programs, because cost should not limit participation): Adapting exercises to low-cost alternatives and connecting her with community resources keeps rehabilitation on track without penalizing her. Postponing strengthening delays recovery, and advising her to cut food spending is inappropriate. A one-time loan helps briefly but does not address the broader barrier.

question: A 52-year-old painter reports lateral elbow pain that began after repainting a house over several days. Gripping a mug and lifting a full kettle are both painful. The physiotherapist suspects lateral epicondylalgia and plans the examination. Which finding is typical of this condition?

options.A: Pain on passive elbow flexion with ulnar paresthesia and a positive elbow flexion test
options.B: Pain on resisted wrist flexion with the elbow extended and tenderness over the medial epicondyle
options.C: Pain on resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended and tenderness over the lateral epicondyle
options.D: Pain with resisted forearm supination and sensory loss over the radial side of the forearm

explanation: The correct answer is C (Pain on resisted wrist extension with the elbow extended and tenderness over the lateral epicondyle): Lateral epicondylalgia involves the common extensor origin, especially extensor carpi radialis brevis, so resisted wrist extension and palpation of the lateral epicondyle reproduce the pain. The medial finding describes the flexor origin, and the other findings suggest radial tunnel or cubital tunnel involvement.

question: A 40-year-old man twisted his ankle on a curb an hour ago. He could not bear weight at the time and can manage only two steps now. Palpation finds no bone tenderness at the malleoli, navicular or fifth metatarsal base. What is the most appropriate decision?

options.A: Repeat palpation after ice application, because swelling can mask tenderness at the landmarks
options.B: Wait three days and reassess walking ability, because early weight-bearing tests are unreliable
options.C: Manage as a sprain without imaging, because bone tenderness is absent at the landmarks
options.D: Refer for radiographs, because inability to take four steps meets the rule

explanation: The correct answer is D (Refer for radiographs, because inability to take four steps meets the rule): The Ottawa rules are positive if the client cannot bear weight for four steps both at the time of injury and at examination, even without bony tenderness. Delaying imaging or relying on absent tenderness would risk missing a fracture.

question: A 24-year-old woman is breathing rapidly and reports tingling in her fingers after a stressful meeting. Her oxygen saturation is normal. The table shows her arterial blood gas. Which interpretation is most appropriate? Her mother is waiting outside and reports no medical history or regular medicines.

options.A: Compensated respiratory alkalosis, because the bicarbonate has fallen to match the low carbon dioxide
options.B: Respiratory acidosis from poor ventilation, because the oxygen level is within the normal reference range
options.C: Acute respiratory alkalosis without metabolic compensation, consistent with acute hyperventilation from anxiety
options.D: Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation, because the pH is high and the carbon dioxide is low

image_params.title: Arterial blood gas, room air
image_params.caption: Sample drawn at rest.

explanation: The correct answer is C (Acute respiratory alkalosis without metabolic compensation, consistent with acute hyperventilation from anxiety): A high pH with a low PaCO2 and normal bicarbonate shows a primary respiratory alkalosis that has not yet been compensated, which fits acute overbreathing. Compensation takes days and would lower the bicarbonate. The alkalosis is from the lungs, not metabolic, and acidosis would show a low pH.

question: A 33-year-old woman who is blind arrives for her first shoulder visit with her guide dog. The receptionist says animals are not allowed in the treatment area and offers to keep the dog in the waiting room. What is the correct response?

options.A: Allow the dog, but have her sign a waiver accepting responsibility for any hygiene concerns
options.B: Allow the guide dog throughout the visit, because human rights law protects service animals
options.C: Keep the dog in the waiting room, because hygiene rules for treatment areas take precedence
options.D: Allow the dog only if she supplies certification papers, because the clinic needs proof

explanation: The correct answer is B (Allow the guide dog throughout the visit, because human rights law protects service animals): Guide dogs are recognized service animals, and excluding one denies equal access to a person with a disability. The role of a guide dog is evident, so proof or a waiver cannot be demanded as a condition. Hygiene rules do not override human rights duties, and separating her from her dog removes her mobility aid in an unfamiliar room.

question: A 3-month-old infant lies supine with hips and knees flexed and feet flat on the table. The left knee sits visibly lower than the right when viewed from the side. His mother also noticed uneven thigh skin folds. Which test and interpretation correctly describe this finding?

options.A: Positive Ortolani sign: the left femoral head has been relocated into the socket by abduction
options.B: Positive Trendelenburg sign: the left hip abductors are weak and the pelvis drops on standing
options.C: Positive Barlow sign: the left hip is dislocatable when adducted with backward pressure
options.D: Positive Galeazzi sign: the left femur appears shortened, consistent with hip dislocation

explanation: The correct answer is D (Positive Galeazzi sign: the left femur appears shortened, consistent with hip dislocation): In the Galeazzi test the knees are flexed with the feet together, and a lower knee on one side indicates apparent femoral shortening from hip dislocation or a short femur. Ortolani and Barlow are maneuvers that involve moving the hip to feel a clunk, not comparing knee heights. Trendelenburg is assessed in standing in a walking child.

question: A 57-year-old man two weeks after a heart attack becomes short of breath during treadmill walking in a cardiac rehabilitation program. He reports chest tightness, tingling in his hands and a fear of dying. His breathing is fast and shallow. Which action should the physiotherapist take first?

options.A: Stop the treadmill, seat him, and check vital signs and symptoms before attributing them to anxiety
options.B: Reassure him and slow the treadmill, because exercise helps reduce anxiety after a cardiac event
options.C: Have him breathe into a paper bag, because it restores carbon dioxide lost through rapid breathing
options.D: Stop the treadmill and coach slow diaphragmatic breathing, because symptoms indicate a panic attack from hyperventilation

explanation: The correct answer is A (Stop the treadmill, seat him, and check vital signs and symptoms before attributing them to anxiety): Chest tightness and breathlessness shortly after a heart attack must be treated as possibly cardiac until vital signs and symptoms are checked. Only once a cardiac cause is reasonably excluded should anxiety management with breathing coaching follow. Continuing exercise is unsafe, and rebreathing into a bag can lower oxygen and is not recommended.

question: A 58-year-old man with aphasia after a stroke is told the clinic accepts bookings only through an online form. His wife phones twice and leaves messages but receives no reply. He misses his first appointment. The physiotherapist learns of this. What is the best response?

options.A: Rebook him online with his wife's help, because the policy applies equally to every client
options.B: Refer him to a clinic with phone booking, because the current system suits others better
options.C: Rebook him by phone as a one-time exception, and keep the online form for everyone else
options.D: Arrange his booking by phone, apologize, and ask management to offer alternative ways to book

explanation: The correct answer is D (Arrange his booking by phone, apologize, and ask management to offer alternative ways to book): A booking system that works only through an online form is a barrier for some clients with disabilities such as aphasia. Arranging his booking, apologizing and asking management for alternative ways to book removes the barrier for him and others. A one-time exception leaves the barrier in place, equal treatment ignores the unequal effect, and referral moves the clinic's duty to accommodate to another provider.

question: A 61-year-old retired mail carrier twisted his knee stepping off a curb yesterday. He has mild effusion, can fully extend and flex 100 degrees, and a negative Ottawa knee assessment. He asks whether to keep his knee elevated and still. Which statement best guides early management?

options.A: Early gentle movement and progressive walking promote recovery, and elevation can ease bothersome swelling
options.B: Keeping the knee still for ten days limits swelling and prevents the injured structures from stretching
options.C: Elevation and ice for the first week is the evidence-based way to prevent chronic effusion
options.D: Waiting for swelling to resolve before bending the knee prevents damage to the joint lining

explanation: The correct answer is A (Early gentle movement and progressive walking promote recovery, and elevation can ease bothersome swelling): Early gentle movement and progressive loading are favoured in soft tissue knee injuries without fracture concern. Elevation can ease discomfort but is not a substitute for activity. Prolonged immobilization and waiting for swelling to settle both delay function.

question: A 71-year-old woman with Parkinson disease takes levodopa every four hours. By three hours after each dose she becomes slow and stiff, and her gait deteriorates noticeably. She wants to plan the week. When should the physiotherapist schedule her most demanding gait training?

options.A: About one hour after a dose, when medication effect is near its peak
options.B: Just before her next dose, so she practises cueing strategies during the wearing-off period
options.C: First thing in the morning before any medication, to build compensatory strategies
options.D: About three hours after a dose, to practise coping strategies as stiffness returns

explanation: The correct answer is A (About one hour after a dose, when medication effect is near its peak): Demanding training is most productive when medication is working, usually around an hour after a dose. Practising in the off period is useful for learning cues, but intensive gait work then is less effective and riskier. Timing therapy to the on period improves performance and safety.

question: A 76-year-old woman with sarcopenia starts a lower limb strengthening program in an outpatient clinic. She lives alone, is otherwise healthy and can attend the clinic on most days. The physiotherapist plans the weekly frequency. Which schedule best supports strength gains while allowing recovery?

options.A: One session per week at high load, because older adults need six days to recover
options.B: Daily sessions at moderate load, because every day training maximizes the stimulus for older muscle
options.C: Two to three sessions per week on non consecutive days, allowing muscle recovery between sessions
options.D: Five sessions per week in blocks of two days, because rest matters only weekly

explanation: The correct answer is C (Two to three sessions per week on non consecutive days, allowing muscle recovery between sessions): Resistance training guidelines support two to three non consecutive days per week for older adults, giving the muscle time to adapt between bouts. Daily training offers little recovery, a single weekly session gives too little stimulus, and consecutive day blocks remove the rest the muscle needs.

question: A 13-year-old boy with asthma completes a treadmill challenge. The chart shows his FEV1 as a percentage of baseline at timed points afterwards, with the 90 percent line marked. His school asks whether the result supports exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: The baseline value of 100 percent shows normal airways, so no exercise precautions are needed
options.B: The partial recovery by thirty minutes cancels the earlier fall, so the result is negative
options.C: A fall of about 20 percent at fifteen minutes exceeds the usual 10 percent criterion
options.D: A fall of about 7 percent at thirty minutes, short of the usual 10 percent criterion

image_params.title: FEV1 after treadmill challenge
image_params.caption: Standardized treadmill challenge

explanation: The correct answer is C (A fall of about 20 percent at fifteen minutes exceeds the usual 10 percent criterion): The lowest value is 80 percent of baseline at fifteen minutes, a fall of about 20 percent, which exceeds the usual 10 percent criterion for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. The thirty minute value is only the recovery point, and recovery does not cancel the earlier fall. A baseline of 100 percent is the reference, not a sign of normal airways.

question: A systematic review of cohort studies suggests a type of footwear reduces knee pain, while one new well-conducted randomized trial found no difference. A physiotherapist must decide how to weigh these sources for a client who asks about the footwear. Which reasoning is best?

options.A: Give the randomized trial more weight for causal questions, while acknowledging the uncertainty
options.B: Ignore the trial because a single study cannot outweigh published review conclusions on its own
options.C: Give the review more weight, because it combines many studies and therefore removes confounding
options.D: Average the two findings equally, since each design answers the same question in the same way

explanation: The correct answer is A (Give the randomized trial more weight for causal questions, while acknowledging the uncertainty): Randomization reduces confounding, which cohort studies cannot do even when pooled, so the trial is stronger for cause and effect. The trial's size still limits certainty. Pooling observational data does not remove confounding.

question: A physiotherapist in an outpatient clinic realizes she applied a hot pack for too long, leaving a small area of redness on a 66-year-old patient's lower back that settled within an hour. She wants to follow good practice. Which element should be included when she discloses this event?

options.A: A factual account of what happened, but any apology waits until the review confirms fault
options.B: An apology and reassurance that the redness is minor, without describing how it happened
options.C: A written description of the event and effects, sent later by the clinic manager
options.D: A factual account of what happened and its effects, plus a sincere apology

explanation: The correct answer is D (A factual account of what happened and its effects, plus a sincere apology): Disclosure standards call for a clear, factual description of the event and its effects, together with a sincere apology, given directly to the patient. Delaying the apology, omitting how the event happened or leaving the account to a later letter withholds information the patient is entitled to and weakens trust.

question: A physiotherapist receives a text from a client's spouse asking how the client's therapy is going. The client consented to appointment reminders by text but never discussed involving the spouse. The physiotherapist is in a private clinic. What should she do?

options.A: Provide a brief update by text, but avoid mentioning the diagnosis or treatment
options.B: Share general progress, because spouses are usually part of the circle of care
options.C: Tell the spouse to ask the client directly, and share only the next appointment time
options.D: Decline to share details until the client has consented to disclosure to the spouse

explanation: The correct answer is D (Decline to share details until the client has consented to disclosure to the spouse): A spouse is not automatically a member of the care team, so personal health information, including appointment times, requires the client's consent. General updates still disclose that the person is a client and how care is going.

question: A 46-year-old welder with lateral elbow pain has completed 12 weeks of loading exercise. The chart plots pain-free grip strength on the affected side, with a reference line for the unaffected side. Before discussing return to full duties, the physiotherapist calculates limb symmetry at week 12. What is the value?

options.A: About 53 percent, because the 16 kilogram gain is divided by the 30 kilogram final value
options.B: About 12 percent, because 4 kilograms divided by 34 kilograms is the deficit
options.C: About 88 percent, because 30 kilograms divided by 34 kilograms gives 0.88
options.D: About 113 percent, because 34 kilograms divided by 30 kilograms gives 1.13

image_params.title: Pain-free grip strength, affected hand
image_params.caption: Dynamometer, second handle position, mean of three trials

explanation: The correct answer is C (About 88 percent, because 30 kilograms divided by 34 kilograms gives 0.88): Limb symmetry is the affected value divided by the unaffected value: 30 divided by 34 is 0.88, or 88 percent. Dividing the other way gives an impossible ratio above 100 percent. The deficit or gain from baseline answers different questions and does not describe symmetry.

question: A 16-year-old goalkeeper, five months after ACL reconstruction, has 95 percent limb symmetry on strength testing but has not been cleared for jumping, and she reports fear of re-injury. Her parents want her to play in the provincial final next week, but she seems unsure. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Tell the parents she is not ready and advise them to keep her out of sport
options.B: Follow the parents' wishes on timing, because they are responsible for decisions affecting a minor's activities
options.C: Clear her for the final with a brace, since strength testing met the return threshold
options.D: Explain safe return criteria and timeline, listen to her concerns, and plan next steps with them

explanation: The correct answer is D (Explain safe return criteria and timeline, listen to her concerns, and plan next steps with them): Return to sport depends on progressive criteria and time after surgery, not strength alone, and she has not yet cleared jumping. The best response informs the family, listens to her fear, and builds a plan with her. Clearing her on one measure is unsafe, and either side simply deciding for her ignores her own voice.

question: A physiotherapist who completed a weekend course in dry needling is told by her clinic owner to begin offering it to clients next week to attract new business. She is unsure whether it falls inside her scope and has not checked her college's position. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Offer it to selected clients after a signed waiver, since the weekend course certificate shows competence
options.B: Check that her liability insurer covers it, then offer it once the clinic owner approves
options.C: Confirm her college permits it and her training meets standards, offering it only once competent
options.D: Complete a second course from the same provider, then begin offering it to clients

explanation: The correct answer is C (Confirm her college permits it and her training meets standards, offering it only once competent): Whether a technique is within scope, and the training required, are set by the college and legislation, and competence must be demonstrated rather than assumed from a short course. A waiver, insurer coverage or employer approval cannot create authority, and more training from the same provider does not answer the scope question.

question: A 62-year-old retired electrician with chronic neck pain rates his average pain at 8 out of 10 at baseline. After six weeks of exercise and education he rates it at 5 out of 10. Using commonly cited thresholds of a 2-point or 30 percent reduction, how should the physiotherapist describe the change?

options.A: Not meaningful, because the final rating of 5 out of 10 still indicates moderate pain
options.B: Not interpretable, because numeric rating scales cannot be compared across different treatment sessions
options.C: Clinically meaningful, because the 3-point drop equals a 37.5 percent reduction and meets both thresholds
options.D: Meaningful by points only, because the 3-point drop equals just 25 percent of baseline

explanation: The correct answer is C (Clinically meaningful, because the 3-point drop equals a 37.5 percent reduction and meets both thresholds): A drop from 8 to 5 is 3 points, and 3 divided by 8 is 37.5 percent, which exceeds both the 2-point and the 30 percent thresholds. The final level of pain does not decide whether the change is meaningful, and numeric rating scales are routinely compared over time.

question: A 29-year-old man recently diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis worries that exercise will trigger relapses and damage his nerves. He has minimal disability and walks without aids. He asks for clear advice about aerobic and strength training. How should the physiotherapist respond?

options.A: Aerobic exercise is helpful but resistance training is harmful, because muscle loading worsens fatigue and spasticity
options.B: Aerobic and resistance exercise is safe in his stage and improves fitness, mood and fatigue
options.C: Only light intensity is safe, because moderate effort raises relapse risk and nerve damage
options.D: Exercise should wait until disability appears, because early disease needs rest to protect myelin

explanation: The correct answer is B (Aerobic and resistance exercise is safe in his stage and improves fitness, mood and fatigue): Evidence shows regular aerobic and resistance exercise is safe for people with mild multiple sclerosis and improves fitness, fatigue and mood without increasing relapse rates. Delaying exercise lets deconditioning develop, and resistance training is also recommended. Intensity is progressed to tolerance rather than restricted to light effort.

question: A 61-year-old woman with a stage 2 cystocele has long-standing constipation and strains hard to pass stools. She sits upright with her feet flat and holds her breath when pushing. She asks how to make bowel movements easier without worsening her prolapse. Which toileting technique should be taught?

options.A: Squeeze the pelvic floor during the movement to support the prolapse while passing stool
options.B: Hold the breath and tighten the abdomen strongly to increase pressure for passing stool
options.C: Lean forward, rest feet on a stool, relax the pelvic floor and breathe out gently
options.D: Sit upright with feet flat and take a deep breath, then push down firmly to start

explanation: The correct answer is C (Lean forward, rest feet on a stool, relax the pelvic floor and breathe out gently): Leaning forward with the feet raised straightens the anorectal angle, and relaxing the pelvic floor with an easy out-breath lets stool pass without straining. Breath holding and pushing raise abdominal pressure and push down on the prolapse, while squeezing the pelvic floor blocks the passage.

question: A 39-year-old carpenter with chronic back pain fears that lifting will damage his spine and avoids it. The physiotherapist plans graded exposure. He rates picking up a pen as 1 out of 10 fear and lifting a toolbox as 8 out of 10. Which first step is appropriate?

options.A: Start with activities he rates as low fear and progress step by step to higher-rated tasks
options.B: Teach him to brace the trunk firmly, then add heavier lifts once fear rating drops
options.C: Begin with lifting the toolbox so that the most feared task is faced and resolved quickly
options.D: Wait until his pain reaches zero, then test low-fear activities to confirm he is safe

explanation: The correct answer is A (Start with activities he rates as low fear and progress step by step to higher-rated tasks): Graded exposure builds a hierarchy from least to most feared activities and moves up as confidence grows. Starting with the toolbox overwhelms him, waiting for zero pain ties activity to symptoms, and bracing hard can reinforce the belief that the spine is fragile.

question: A 25-year-old man with cystic fibrosis is cycling in an outpatient exercise program when he suddenly reports sharp right-sided chest pain and worsening breathlessness. His saturation falls from 94 to 88 percent and breath sounds on the right seem reduced. What should the physiotherapist do first?

options.A: Start airway clearance with huffing to clear a mucus plug, because retained secretions explain these findings
options.B: Stop exercise, keep him upright, apply oxygen per protocol and call urgently for medical help
options.C: Lie him flat and recheck vital signs for ten minutes before deciding on medical help
options.D: Coach pursed-lip breathing and resume cycling at lower resistance, because exertional chest pain often eases

explanation: The correct answer is B (Stop exercise, keep him upright, apply oxygen per protocol and call urgently for medical help): Sudden pleuritic chest pain, desaturation and reduced breath sounds in a young person with cystic fibrosis suggest a pneumothorax, which is a medical emergency. Exercise stops, he stays upright, oxygen is applied per protocol and help is called urgently. Waiting, clearing secretions or resuming exercise delays treatment.

question: An 84-year-old woman with advanced dementia in a long-term care home is referred for a progressive strengthening program and a splinting trial. The physiotherapist determines that she cannot understand the proposed treatment. Her son holds a valid power of attorney for personal care. Who should give consent for the treatment?

options.A: The referring physician, because the referral order transfers consent authority for treatment to the physician
options.B: Her son as substitute decision-maker, after receiving the same information the client would have received
options.C: Her son, without further information, because his power of attorney already covers all future care decisions
options.D: The client herself, using simple language, because dementia alone does not remove her consent rights

explanation: The correct answer is B (Her son as substitute decision-maker, after receiving the same information the client would have received): When a client lacks capacity for a treatment decision, a legally authorized substitute decision-maker gives or refuses consent after receiving the information the client would have received. Because the physiotherapist found she cannot understand this treatment, she cannot consent herself. A referral or care staff do not hold that authority, and the son must be informed before deciding.

question: Four clients arrive for their scheduled hydrotherapy sessions at the same pool. All four have musculoskeletal conditions and were medically stable at their last review. The physiotherapist performs a pre-session screen of each. Which client should be asked to postpone entering the pool today?

options.A: A 72-year-old with controlled hypertension whose blood pressure measured 138/84 just before entering the pool today
options.B: A 55-year-old with well-controlled type 2 diabetes who ate a snack one hour earlier
options.C: A 45-year-old with stress incontinence who emptied her bladder and showered before entering the pool
options.D: A 60-year-old with a fever of 38.5 degrees C and generalized body aches since this morning

explanation: The correct answer is D (A 60-year-old with a fever of 38.5 degrees C and generalized body aches since this morning): An active fever suggests infection and is a reason to postpone pool exercise, since warm water adds thermal stress and the client could spread infection to others. A blood pressure of 138/84, controlled diabetes with a recent snack, and stress incontinence managed by emptying the bladder are routine screening findings that do not require postponement.

question: A 76-year-old woman living at home has had two falls this year, walks with a cane, and can stand unsupported for thirty seconds. Her physiotherapist designs a falls-prevention exercise plan. Which dose of exercise best reflects the evidence for reducing falls in older adults?

options.A: Gentle balance exercises totalling thirty minutes weekly, stopped once the client feels steadier on her feet
options.B: A twelve-session balance course delivered once, since short courses produce lasting falls reduction on their own
options.C: Challenging balance exercises totalling around three hours weekly, continued long term alongside strengthening
options.D: Seated upper limb strengthening three times weekly, since arm strength protects against loss of balance

explanation: The correct answer is C (Challenging balance exercises totalling around three hours weekly, continued long term alongside strengthening): Trials show that falls fall most when exercise challenges balance, totals about three hours per week, and continues over time. Brief or gentle programs, upper limb work without balance challenge and one-off short courses do not provide enough dose or specificity to keep reducing falls.

question: A manager tells a physiotherapist that her average visit time is 15 minutes longer than her peers'. Her caseload includes many clients with dementia and complex mobility needs, and her outcomes have been good. She disagrees with the comparison. Which response is most professional?

options.A: Shorten every visit by 15 minutes right away to match the peer average visit time
options.B: Reject the feedback because productivity measures cannot capture the quality of clinical care
options.C: Ask to be compared only with colleagues who have similar caseloads, and decline other data
options.D: Share data on her caseload complexity and ask how time is measured, staying open to change

explanation: The correct answer is D (Share data on her caseload complexity and ask how time is measured, staying open to change): Professional receipt of feedback includes presenting relevant evidence, asking how the comparison was made, and remaining willing to improve efficiency where safe. Cutting visit time reflexively risks quality, and dismissing the measure or limiting the comparison group defends against the feedback without engaging with it.

question: A college practice advisor reviews a physiotherapist's clinical records during a routine audit and notes that many of her handwritten entries are difficult to read. She asks what the standard requires of entries in a client record. Which requirement applies?

options.A: Entries must be legible and dated, but signing is needed only for major changes
options.B: Entries must be typed, since handwritten entries are not acceptable in clinical records
options.C: Entries must be legible, dated and signed, so another professional can understand them
options.D: Entries must be dated and signed, and may use personal abbreviations the author understands

explanation: The correct answer is C (Entries must be legible, dated and signed, so another professional can understand them): Records exist so that others can understand the care provided, which requires legibility, dates and an identifiable author. Handwriting is acceptable if legible, and a signature is required on each entry. Personal abbreviations that only the author knows defeat the purpose of a shared record.

question: A 66 year old man with a tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation is ready to march on the spot at the bedside. The physiotherapist sets a stop rule of 20 beats per minute above his resting heart rate of 84. At which heart rate should she stop?

options.A: At 112 beats per minute, because the limit is one third above the resting rate
options.B: At 131 beats per minute, because 85 percent of his age predicted maximum is the limit
options.C: At 104 beats per minute, because 20 above the resting rate of 84 is the limit
options.D: At 101 beats per minute, because the limit is 20 percent above his resting rate

explanation: The correct answer is C (At 104 beats per minute, because 20 above the resting rate of 84 is the limit): The rule adds 20 beats to the resting rate of 84, giving 104. The other values come from applying a percentage to the resting rate or using a percentage of age predicted maximum, which would be different rules from the one the physiotherapist set.

question: A 63-year-old man is finishing phase II cardiac rehabilitation and wants to keep exercising at home. He understands his heart rate zone but sometimes ignores symptoms when he feels rushed or pressed for time. Which instruction best promotes safe independent exercise for him afterwards?

options.A: Push through mild chest discomfort if his pulse stays within the training zone he learned
options.B: Exercise most days at a comfortable pace and stop only if his pulse exceeds his zone
options.C: Exercise most days at his learned level, and check symptoms only after each session ends
options.D: Exercise most days at his learned exertion level, with warm-up, cool-down and stop rules for symptoms

explanation: The correct answer is D (Exercise most days at his learned exertion level, with warm-up, cool-down and stop rules for symptoms): A safe home program uses regular moderate activity, a warm-up, a cool-down and clear rules to stop for warning symptoms. Using the pulse as the only stop signal, or checking symptoms after the session, misses chest discomfort that can occur within the target zone. Pushing through discomfort is unsafe, and a normal pulse does not make symptoms safe.

question: A 40-year-old runner starts heel-drop exercises for midportion Achilles tendinopathy. During the first week she scores her pain as 4 out of 10 during exercise, and it is back to baseline by the next morning. She asks whether she should stop. What guidance is most appropriate?

options.A: Continue loading only when pain scores zero at rest and during every single repetition performed
options.B: Stop each set at the first sign of any pain, since discomfort signals ongoing tissue damage
options.C: Pain up to five out of ten during loading is acceptable if it settles by morning
options.D: Continue loading while pain rises, because stronger pain shows a greater stimulus to the tendon

explanation: The correct answer is C (Pain up to five out of ten during loading is acceptable if it settles by morning): Tendinopathy loading programs commonly allow moderate pain during exercise if it does not escalate and returns to baseline by the next day, since this indicates tolerable load. Zero pain is not required, and rising pain that does not settle signals excessive load.

question: A physiotherapist who once enjoyed her work now feels drained by the end of each morning, speaks sarcastically about clients, and doubts that her treatments help anyone. These feelings began after a year of heavy caseloads. Which concept best describes this combination of experiences?

options.A: Normal adjustment reaction, marked by short-term stress, because new demands briefly strain coping
options.B: Compassion satisfaction, marked by fulfillment, because helping others produces lasting professional rewards
options.C: Burnout, marked by exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness, because chronic stress overwhelms coping
options.D: Moral injury, caused by acting against personal values, because workplace limits conflict with conscience

explanation: The correct answer is C (Burnout, marked by exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness, because chronic stress overwhelms coping): Exhaustion, cynicism and a sense of ineffectiveness are the core features of burnout caused by prolonged workplace stress. Compassion satisfaction is the opposite experience, and moral injury arises from acting against one's values rather than from overload. An adjustment reaction is time-limited, while her symptoms have continued for a year.

question: A 50-year-old man with a known latex allergy attends a clinic for a program of resisted elastic band exercises and gait practice. Several items are used each session: bands, a goniometer, a vinyl plinth and aluminum crutches. Which item is most likely to contain latex and should be replaced?

options.A: Vinyl-covered plinth surfaces that are wiped down between clients in the treatment room each day
options.B: Standard stretch bands made from natural rubber, which are used for resisted exercise at home
options.C: Silicone rubber tips on the aluminum crutches, which are used for gait practice daily
options.D: Aluminum forearm crutches fitted with gel hand grips that are used for supervised gait practice daily

explanation: The correct answer is B (Standard stretch bands made from natural rubber, which are used for resisted exercise at home): Many resistance bands are made from natural rubber latex, which can trigger a reaction in an allergic client, so a latex-free band is used. Vinyl coverings, silicone tips and gel grips are synthetic materials and are not typical latex sources, though product labels should still be checked.

question: A 26-year-old athlete is eight months after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. Manual muscle testing grades both quadriceps as 5 out of 5, yet he reports the operated leg feels weaker during jumping. What is the most appropriate next step for strength assessment?

options.A: Repeat manual muscle testing in a different position with knee flexed, because position explains the mismatch
options.B: Accept the grades and clear him for return to sport, because both legs scored identically
options.C: Measure thigh circumference with a tape at standard sites, because girth directly reflects maximal muscle strength
options.D: Quantify force with hand-held dynamometry and compare limbs, because manual testing misses high-level deficits

explanation: The correct answer is D (Quantify force with hand-held dynamometry and compare limbs, because manual testing misses high-level deficits): Manual muscle testing has a ceiling effect at high grades and is insensitive to side-to-side deficits, so objective force measurement with a dynamometer is needed. Girth does not measure strength directly, and clearing him on identical grades ignores his report.

question: A 34-year-old man with a complete T10 spinal cord injury will be discharged home in three days. The team has ordered a wheelchair and a transfer bench. His home has three entry steps and a narrow bathroom door. What should the physiotherapist arrange before discharge?

options.A: A home visit with the patient and family to practise entry, transfers, and bathroom access
options.B: Delay discharge until a ramp and widened bathroom door are installed, since access must be complete
options.C: Ask the community therapist to assess the home after discharge, since hospital staff rarely visit homes
options.D: Provide a written home program for upper body strengthening and wheelchair skills, and book outpatient follow-up

explanation: The correct answer is A (A home visit with the patient and family to practise entry, transfers, and bathroom access): A home visit lets the team test the real entry, the bench transfer and the bathroom door with him and his family, and identify the modifications still needed. Delaying until all work is done may not be necessary, and a written program or later assessment leaves safety problems untested on his first day home.

question: While changing the bedding to place a transfer belt, a physiotherapist is punctured on the finger by a lancet left in the sheets of a client known to have hepatitis C. Bleeding is minimal and the client is waiting for the session. What should the physiotherapist do first?

options.A: Wash the wound with soap and water, finish the session, then report to the supervisor
options.B: Wash the wound well, then report only if the client's hepatitis test result is positive
options.C: Wash the wound with soap and water, then report to occupational health right away for follow-up
options.D: Apply an adhesive bandage and complete the treatment, then tell the supervisor the next morning

explanation: The correct answer is C (Wash the wound with soap and water, then report to occupational health right away for follow-up): Washing with soap and water removes contaminated material, and reporting to occupational health right away allows time-sensitive risk assessment and follow-up testing. Finishing the session before reporting delays that assessment, and reporting only on a positive result ignores that the source is already known to carry hepatitis C. Covering the wound with a bandage and waiting until the next day loses the window for follow-up.

question: A 20-year-old volleyball player is cleared to return to play six weeks after a lateral ankle sprain. She asks the physiotherapist whether a brace or tape is better for preventing another sprain during games. Which recommendation is best supported for an athlete with a previous sprain?

options.A: A soft elastic sleeve, because compression alone gives the same stability as a stiffer device
options.B: A lace-up or semi-rigid brace, because external support lowers the rate of repeat sprains
options.C: Athletic tape applied once before warm-up, because it keeps its full stiffness throughout play
options.D: No external support, because bracing weakens the peroneal muscles over a full season

explanation: The correct answer is B (A lace-up or semi-rigid brace, because external support lowers the rate of repeat sprains): Evidence supports lace-up or semi-rigid braces for reducing recurrent sprains in athletes with a prior injury, and braces maintain their support through a game. Tape loses much of its stiffness within the first part of exercise, bracing has not been shown to weaken the peroneals, and a soft sleeve offers little mechanical support.

question: A 60-year-old man has shoulder abduction of 95 degrees actively and 130 degrees passively, measured twice with consistent results. Passive overpressure at the end of passive range produces no pain, and his scapular movement is normal. Which explanation best fits these findings?

options.A: Capsular restriction of the glenohumeral joint, because range is limited in both active and passive movements
options.B: Measurement error between the two trials, because goniometric readings commonly vary by more than 30 degrees
options.C: A contractile or neural problem limiting active movement, because passive range exceeds active range
options.D: A bony block at the acromion, because motion stops short of full elevation on both tests

explanation: The correct answer is C (A contractile or neural problem limiting active movement, because passive range exceeds active range): When passive range is greater than active range, the limit is in the contractile tissue or its nerve supply, such as weakness or pain inhibition, not in the joint. Capsular or bony restrictions would limit passive movement too, and repeatable measures rule out a 35 degree error.

question: A 79-year-old woman with moderate dementia has been found incapable of consenting to a rehabilitation program. Her son and daughter disagree about starting it. The chart shows she named her daughter as attorney for personal care years ago. Whose consent should the physiotherapist seek?

options.A: The patient herself, because capacity is assessed per treatment and her wishes remain decisive
options.B: The daughter, the appointed substitute decision maker, who must follow her mother's known wishes
options.C: Both children jointly, because adult children share equal authority and the family should agree together
options.D: The physician, who found her incapable and therefore may direct the rehabilitation plan on her behalf

explanation: The correct answer is B (The daughter, the appointed substitute decision maker, who must follow her mother's known wishes): When a person is found incapable, the legally authorized substitute decision maker consents, and a person she appointed ahead of time ranks above siblings. That person must act on her prior wishes. Physicians assess capacity but do not consent for the patient, and she has already been found incapable for this decision.

question: A physiotherapist leads a six-week arthritis self-management group in a community centre. A new volunteer asks what makes this kind of program different from a standard exercise class run by a clinic. Which element is a defining feature of self-management programs?

options.A: Supervised group exercise with progressive resistance so participants build strength and joint mobility
options.B: Teaching problem solving, goal setting and action planning skills so participants manage daily demands
options.C: Delivering disease information in lectures by specialists so participants understand the underlying pathology
options.D: Running peer-led social meetings where participants share experiences and encouragement together

explanation: The correct answer is B (Teaching problem solving, goal setting and action planning skills so participants manage daily demands): Self-management programs build the participant's own skills in problem solving, decision making, goal setting and action planning so that daily demands of the condition can be handled independently. Supervised exercise describes the standard clinic class the volunteer is comparing against. Specialist lectures supply knowledge without building skills, and peer social meetings offer support but do not by themselves teach the skills that define the approach.

question: A 47-year-old bus driver with chronic plantar heel pain was prescribed five home exercise sessions weekly. The chart shows his completed sessions and pain scores across eight weeks. He tells the physiotherapist he is busy and does not think the exercises are helping. What should the physiotherapist do first?

options.A: Refer him back to his physician, because poor response to exercise suggests another diagnosis
options.B: Explain that pain rose as sessions fell, then restate the original five-session plan
options.C: Explore his barriers and beliefs, then negotiate a realistic program he feels able to complete
options.D: Change to a new exercise set immediately, because the current set has not worked

image_params.title: Home Sessions Completed and Pain Over Eight Weeks
image_params.y_label: Sessions per week or pain score (0 to 10)
image_params.caption: Client diary and clinic pain ratings

explanation: The correct answer is C (Explore his barriers and beliefs, then negotiate a realistic program he feels able to complete): The chart shows pain improving while he exercised and returning as sessions dropped, so the program was working when done. His low adherence and doubt are the problem to address, best by understanding barriers and agreeing a feasible plan together. Repeating the plan, changing exercises or referring ignores the adherence issue.

question: A 33-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has taken prednisone daily for four years. For three weeks she has had deep groin pain with weight bearing and limited hip internal rotation. Her lupus blood tests are stable and imaging is pending. How should the physiotherapist proceed?

options.A: Attribute it to a lupus arthritis flare and increase aerobic exercise to reduce joint inflammation
options.B: Suspect avascular necrosis and inform her physician about imaging needs, limiting impact loading meanwhile
options.C: Progress closed-chain squats and jumping to strengthen the muscles that support the hip joint
options.D: Treat as a hip flexor strain with stretching, because strain commonly causes groin pain

explanation: The correct answer is B (Suspect avascular necrosis and inform her physician about imaging needs, limiting impact loading meanwhile): Long-term corticosteroids and lupus are risk factors for avascular necrosis of the femoral head, which presents as deep groin pain with loss of internal rotation. Impact loading could cause collapse, so early communication and protected loading are needed. Strain or flare explanations are less likely given stable disease.

question: A 52-year-old woman fractured her tibial shaft and is two weeks post nailing. She smokes a pack of cigarettes daily and asks why her surgeon keeps asking about it. Which explanation by the physiotherapist about smoking and fracture healing is most accurate?

options.A: Nicotine reduces blood flow and bone-forming cell activity, raising the risk of delayed healing
options.B: Smoking mainly slows skin wound healing, with little direct effect on the bone itself
options.C: Smoking causes the fixation hardware to loosen over time, which delays the start of weight-bearing
options.D: Smoking lowers calcium absorption from food, which is the main reason fractured bones heal slowly

explanation: The correct answer is A (Nicotine reduces blood flow and bone-forming cell activity, raising the risk of delayed healing): Nicotine and other smoke components impair blood supply and osteoblast function, so smokers have higher rates of delayed union and nonunion. The effect is on bone itself, not only the skin, and it is not mainly explained by calcium intake or hardware loosening.

question: A 51-year-old woman with a unilateral vestibular hypofunction after neuritis has persistent dizziness during head turns. She avoids moving her head, and her gaze blurs when walking. The physiotherapist selects an exercise to promote adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex. Which exercise is most appropriate?

options.A: Fix the gaze on a still target while turning the head side to side daily
options.B: Rest with the head still until the dizziness fades, then resume head movements gradually later
options.C: Lie down quickly on each side in turn, holding until the dizziness settles to clear debris
options.D: Follow a moving target with the eyes while keeping the head still, repeated several times daily

explanation: The correct answer is A (Fix the gaze on a still target while turning the head side to side daily): Adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex is driven by keeping the image of a stationary target steady on the retina while the head moves, which creates the error signal needed to recalibrate the reflex. Head-still eye tracking trains smooth pursuit instead, avoidance delays compensation, and lying down on each side is a habituation exercise for positional vertigo.

question: A 66-year-old man is asked to tap his thumb and index finger together as large and fast as possible. After a few taps, the movements become progressively smaller and slower, with brief hesitations. Which cardinal feature of Parkinson disease does this best demonstrate?

options.A: Postural instability, shown by loss of balance recovery during repeated hand movements
options.B: Bradykinesia, shown by slowing and shrinking amplitude as the repeated movement continues
options.C: Resting tremor, shown by rhythmic oscillation that interrupts the voluntary tapping movement
options.D: Rigidity, shown by a steady increase in resistance as the movement is repeated

explanation: The correct answer is B (Bradykinesia, shown by slowing and shrinking amplitude as the repeated movement continues): Bradykinesia is slowness of movement with a progressive decrease in speed and amplitude on repetition, called the sequence effect. Rigidity is resistance to passive movement, tremor appears at rest, and postural instability is a balance problem. None of these produce shrinking repeated taps.

question: A 70-year-old man with bilateral vestibular hypofunction starts standing balance exercises on a compliant surface with eyes closed at home. He lives alone and sways noticeably. He has had no falls so far this year. Which safety setup should the physiotherapist teach?

options.A: Practise beside his bed with the lights off, so he can lie down quickly if dizzy
options.B: Use a corner with a sturdy chair ahead, a wall beside him and his phone close
options.C: Hold onto a chair back with both hands throughout, to eliminate sway while eyes are closed
options.D: Practise in an open room on foam so he can sway freely, with furniture cleared away

explanation: The correct answer is B (Use a corner with a sturdy chair ahead, a wall beside him and his phone close): Exercises that challenge balance should be practised in a corner with a stable support in front and a wall to the side, so he can catch himself, with a phone within reach because he lives alone. An open room offers nothing to grab, holding on throughout removes the challenge, and turning lights off removes visual input and raises fall risk.

question: A 68-year-old man has had burning, band-like pain along the left side of his rib cage for three days. He expected a muscle strain. The photograph shows his skin. He asks if treatment can start with hands-on soft tissue work today. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Treat as thoracic facet pain with mobilization, since the pain is band-like and one-sided
options.B: Apply heat and electrical stimulation over the rash, since modalities ease chest wall nerve pain
options.C: Suspect herpes zoster, avoid skin contact and refer him promptly to a physician for assessment
options.D: Treat as an intercostal strain with rib stretching and manual therapy, since muscle injury looks similar

image_params.prompt: Photograph of the bare upper back and side of an adult torso, a single band of grouped small red blisters and redness on one side following a line around the ribs and not crossing the midline, neutral clinic lighting, no face visible, no text
image_params.caption: Skin of the trunk

explanation: The correct answer is C (Suspect herpes zoster, avoid skin contact and refer him promptly to a physician for assessment): A unilateral dermatomal band of pain with grouped vesicles that does not cross the midline is typical of herpes zoster. Early antiviral treatment depends on prompt medical assessment, and the lesions can transmit virus to non-immune contacts. Manual therapy or modalities over the rash would be inappropriate.

question: A physiotherapist in a community falls clinic plans to use the Functional Gait Assessment with a 73-year-old man who walks independently but feels unsteady when turning his head. She wants to explain the test to a student. Which description of its structure and scoring is correct?

options.A: Fourteen tasks, each scored from 0 to 4, giving a maximum of 56 points
options.B: Ten walking tasks, each scored from 0 to 3, giving a maximum of 30 points
options.C: Fourteen tasks, each scored from 0 to 2, giving a maximum of 28 points
options.D: Three timed tasks, scored in seconds, with longer times indicating poorer gait performance

explanation: The correct answer is B (Ten walking tasks, each scored from 0 to 3, giving a maximum of 30 points): The Functional Gait Assessment has ten items such as walking with head turns, stepping over obstacles and walking backward, each scored 0 to 3 for a total of 30. The Berg has 14 items scored 0 to 4, and the Mini-BESTest has 14 items scored 0 to 2. Scores of 22 or less out of 30 have been associated with fall risk in older adults.

question: A 75-year-old woman with dementia usually walks independently and is mildly confused. Over two days she has become drowsy and inattentive, with a fever of 38.4 degrees Celsius. She cannot follow her usual walking routine today. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Shorten the session to ten minutes of seated exercise and monitor her afterward
options.B: Proceed with a gentle walk, since the change is likely progression of her dementia
options.C: Hold the session and alert nursing and the physician about possible delirium and infection
options.D: Encourage fluids and rest, then reassess her mobility tomorrow before notifying anyone else

explanation: The correct answer is C (Hold the session and alert nursing and the physician about possible delirium and infection): Acute inattention, drowsiness and fever developing over days suggest delirium, often caused by infection, which is medically urgent and differs from the slow course of dementia. The physiotherapist holds treatment and reports the change so it can be assessed today. A shortened seated session or a gentle walk still treats her as if nothing has changed, and waiting a day to report delays care for a potentially serious condition.

question: A 47-year-old man has mild non-pitting swelling of the fingers after a wrist sprain 2 weeks ago. There is no infection, skin breakdown or circulatory concern. The physiotherapist decides to use an elastic wrap on one swollen finger. How should the wrap be applied?

options.A: From the finger middle outward in both directions, covering the nail bed to keep it warm
options.B: From finger base to tip with firm pressure, to push fluid out toward the end
options.C: From the fingertip toward the base with very tight pressure, to maximize fluid movement
options.D: From fingertip to base with firm but not constricting pressure, leaving the nail bed visible

explanation: The correct answer is D (From fingertip to base with firm but not constricting pressure, leaving the nail bed visible): Distal-to-proximal wrapping encourages fluid movement toward the hand and avoids trapping edema at the tip. Pressure should be firm but not constricting, and the nail bed stays visible so circulation can be checked.

question: A physiotherapist registered in Alberta is asked to treat, by video, a client who lives in Ontario and is visiting family in Alberta only occasionally. The client lives in Ontario for most of the year. The physiotherapist is not registered in Ontario. What should she do before agreeing?

options.A: Confirm the registration requirements of the college in the client's province before providing virtual care there
options.B: Provide only general education by video, since that falls outside provincial licensure rules in every province
options.C: Proceed after obtaining signed written consent from the client that waives all provincial registration requirements
options.D: Proceed, since her Alberta registration covers physiotherapy delivered by video to clients anywhere in Canada

explanation: The correct answer is A (Confirm the registration requirements of the college in the client's province before providing virtual care there): Virtual care is generally considered to take place where the client is located, so the regulator in that province decides what registration is required. A client's consent cannot waive licensure rules, and a general exemption for education is not something to assume.

question: A new physiotherapy assistant on a mixed medical and surgical unit asks what routine practices mean in a rehabilitation hospital. The physiotherapist explains that they are applied to all clients, whether or not an infection is suspected. Which description of routine practices is correct?

options.A: Gloves for all client contact, with hand hygiene needed only if the gloves are soiled
options.B: A cleaning schedule set by environmental services, followed by clinical staff during outbreaks
options.C: Extra measures such as a private room and a gown for clients with confirmed infection
options.D: Point-of-care risk assessment guiding hand hygiene, PPE and cleaning for every client contact

explanation: The correct answer is D (Point-of-care risk assessment guiding hand hygiene, PPE and cleaning for every client contact): Routine practices are the baseline infection prevention measures used with every client at all times. They rest on a point-of-care risk assessment and include hand hygiene, appropriate PPE, and cleaning of the environment and equipment. Additional precautions are layered on top for specific infections, and gloves never replace hand hygiene.

question: A 42-year-old administrative assistant with chronic pain completes Part A of the Central Sensitization Inventory and scores 52 out of 100 at her first visit. The physiotherapist wants to interpret the result carefully. Which statement best describes how this score should be used?

options.A: It indicates severe peripheral tissue damage, so imaging should be requested before treatment continues
options.B: It exceeds the common cut-off of 40, so it confirms a diagnosis without clinical correlation
options.C: It exceeds the common cut-off of 40, so it supports sensitization features alongside clinical findings
options.D: It falls below the common cut-off of 40, so central sensitization features are unlikely

explanation: The correct answer is C (It exceeds the common cut-off of 40, so it supports sensitization features alongside clinical findings): A score of 40 or more on the Central Sensitization Inventory is commonly used to suggest sensitization-related symptoms, so 52 supports that possibility. The inventory is a screening questionnaire, not a diagnostic test, and must be combined with examination findings. It does not measure tissue damage.

question: During a community walking program, a 67-year-old man with insulin-treated diabetes becomes confused, then drowsy, and cannot follow commands or swallow safely. A glucose meter reads 2.1 mmol/L. There is no glucagon on site and a phone is available. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Call emergency services, place him in the recovery position, and give nothing by mouth
options.B: Wait five minutes in sitting to see whether he rouses before calling for help
options.C: Give small sips of juice, then call emergency services if he has not improved
options.D: Walk him slowly to the nearest bench and give glucose tablets to chew once seated

explanation: The correct answer is A (Call emergency services, place him in the recovery position, and give nothing by mouth): Severe hypoglycemia with impaired swallowing needs glucagon or intravenous glucose, so emergency services are called and he is positioned to protect his airway. Giving fluids or tablets to someone who cannot swallow safely risks aspiration. Waiting or walking him delays treatment of a life-threatening problem.

question: A 29-year-old man comes to clinic with three days of progressive leg weakness after a flu-like illness. Light touch and pinprick sensation are normal above the level of his umbilicus and clearly reduced below it. Which dermatome marks the upper edge of his reduced sensation?

options.A: T7, because the xiphoid process is supplied by the seventh thoracic dermatome
options.B: T4, because the nipple line is supplied by the fourth thoracic dermatome
options.C: T10, because the umbilicus is supplied by the tenth thoracic dermatome
options.D: L1, because the inguinal ligament is supplied by the first lumbar dermatome

explanation: The correct answer is C (T10, because the umbilicus is supplied by the tenth thoracic dermatome): The umbilicus is the landmark for the T10 dermatome, so normal sensation above it and reduced sensation below it localizes the sensory level to T10. The nipple line is T4, the xiphoid process is T7 and the inguinal ligament region is L1. A clear sensory level with new weakness and a recent infection is a reason for urgent medical referral.

question: A 30 year old woman at 20 weeks of an uncomplicated pregnancy exercises on a treadmill while the physiotherapist supervises. She is breathing harder and feels warm, then notices a gush of clear fluid running down her legs. Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Reduce treadmill speed and reassess in ten minutes, because stress urinary incontinence is common in pregnancy
options.B: Stop exercise and arrange prompt medical assessment, because leaking fluid may indicate ruptured membranes
options.C: Have her empty her bladder and resume exercise, because urinary leakage is common at this stage
options.D: Cool her down and monitor for 15 minutes, because overheating can cause sudden sweating and wetness

explanation: The correct answer is B (Stop exercise and arrange prompt medical assessment, because leaking fluid may indicate ruptured membranes): A sudden gush of clear fluid during pregnancy is a warning sign of amniotic fluid leakage, and exercise should stop with prompt medical assessment. Urinary leakage is common, but attributing it without assessment risks missing membrane rupture, and waiting or resuming exercise delays care.

question: A 13-year-old soccer player has pain and a bony prominence at the tibial tubercle, worse with kicking and jumping. He grew 6 cm this year and has no knee swelling or locking. The area is tender to touch, and resisted knee extension reproduces the pain. Which condition is most likely?

options.A: Patellar tendinopathy, because jumping overloads the tendon at the lower pole of the patella
options.B: Iliotibial band friction syndrome, because repetitive flexion and extension irritates the band over the lateral femur
options.C: Osgood-Schlatter disease, because quadriceps traction on the tibial tubercle apophysis causes pain in growing athletes
options.D: Pes anserine bursitis, because kicking irritates the bursa on the medial side of the upper tibia

explanation: The correct answer is C (Osgood-Schlatter disease, because quadriceps traction on the tibial tubercle apophysis causes pain in growing athletes): Pain and a prominence at the tibial tubercle in a growing athlete, worse with jumping and resisted extension, define Osgood-Schlatter disease. Patellar tendinopathy is typically at the patellar pole, pes anserine bursitis is medial and below the joint line, and iliotibial band syndrome is lateral.

question: A new physiotherapist joins a spinal cord injury unit and notices that nurses, occupational therapists, and physiotherapists each teach patients transfers using slightly different methods, which confuses patients. One patient asks which method he should follow. Which action best promotes consistent care across the team?

options.A: Agree on one transfer method with the team at a meeting, clarifying roles, and document it
options.B: Ask the unit manager to choose one method and email it to all staff members
options.C: Make physiotherapy the sole teacher of transfers and have others refer all questions to it
options.D: Let each profession teach transfers separately, then compare patient feedback later to choose one method

explanation: The correct answer is A (Agree on one transfer method with the team at a meeting, clarifying roles, and document it): Consistent teaching comes from the team agreeing together on one method, clarifying who does what, and writing it down so every shift uses it. A directive from the manager skips team input and role clarity, so it is less likely to be followed. Making one profession the only teacher ignores that transfers happen on every shift, and letting each profession keep its own method prolongs the confusion while feedback is gathered.

question: A 48-year-old woman six weeks after COVID-19 is walking in the corridor during a rehabilitation session. She suddenly reports sharp chest pain on breathing in. Her heart rate rises to 118 beats per minute, saturation falls from 96% to 90%, and her left calf is swollen and tender. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Seat her to rest and recheck vital signs in 30 minutes before referral
options.B: Stop activity, seat her, and call for emergency medical help for suspected pulmonary embolism
options.C: Stop activity, seat her, and arrange a physician visit for chest wall strain
options.D: Coach pursed-lip breathing and resume walking once saturation returns above 94 percent

explanation: The correct answer is B (Stop activity, seat her, and call for emergency medical help for suspected pulmonary embolism): Pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, new desaturation and a swollen tender calf after COVID-19 point to deep vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism, which is an emergency requiring activity to stop and help to be called now. Waiting half an hour to recheck delays treatment of a possible clot. Attributing the findings to chest wall strain underestimates the calf and oxygen findings, and resuming walking after breathing coaching could dislodge a clot.

question: A 46-year-old man with neck pain after a rear-end collision completes a craniocervical flexion test. He raises the pressure from 22 to 30 mmHg and uses his sternocleidomastoid strongly at the 28 mmHg stage. At which stage should training start?

options.A: At 28 mmHg, the stage where strong sternocleidomastoid effort appeared, using ten-second holds to build endurance
options.B: At 22 mmHg, the lowest stage tested, using one-second holds to avoid straining the painful neck
options.C: At 30 mmHg, the highest stage reached, using ten-second holds to build deep flexor capacity quickly
options.D: At 26 mmHg, the last stage held without excessive superficial muscle activity, using ten-second holds

explanation: The correct answer is D (At 26 mmHg, the last stage held without excessive superficial muscle activity, using ten-second holds): Training begins at the highest stage performed with good control and without dominant superficial muscle use. Training at stages that rely on sternocleidomastoid reinforces compensation, while the lowest stage offers too little challenge.

question: A physiotherapist examining a 34-year-old runner with shin pain finds focal tenderness over the tibial shaft and pain on hopping. The sports physician's note says shin splints and clears running. The runner plans a race in five days. What should the physiotherapist do?

options.A: Treat it as shin splints for now and re-evaluate after the race is over
options.B: Contact the physician about the focal tenderness and hopping pain, and request imaging first
options.C: Advise the runner to skip the race and stop activity, without informing the physician
options.D: Follow the physician's clearance, since diagnosis belongs to the physician and her role is to treat

explanation: The correct answer is B (Contact the physician about the focal tenderness and hopping pain, and request imaging first): Focal bony tenderness and pain on hopping suggest a possible tibial stress fracture, which differs from diffuse shin splints and changes the plan. The physiotherapist should communicate her findings directly and request further investigation. Staying silent, acting without informing the physician, or waiting until after the race ignores a risk of complete fracture.

question: A 50-year-old man has deep burns to the left axilla and lateral chest on hospital day four. He lies in bed with his left arm held against his side and the shoulder internally rotated. Which shoulder position best prevents an axillary contracture?

options.A: Abduction of 30 degrees with internal rotation, because it avoids any stretch over the burn
options.B: Adduction against the chest in a sling, because it protects the grafted skin from tension
options.C: Abduction of about 90 degrees with slight external rotation, using an arm trough or airplane splint
options.D: Forward flexion of 90 degrees with the arm across the chest, because it unloads the axilla

explanation: The correct answer is C (Abduction of about 90 degrees with slight external rotation, using an arm trough or airplane splint): Holding the arm abducted to about 90 degrees with slight external rotation keeps the axillary skin lengthened during healing. Adduction, minimal abduction or crossing the chest shorten the burned tissue and encourage contracture.

question: A 33-year-old stock clerk lifts boxes from the floor to a shelf many times per shift and has started to notice back tightness at the end of the day. He asks the physiotherapist for one principle that reduces low back loading during lifting. Which advice is most accurate?

options.A: Keep the load close to the body, because a shorter lever arm lowers spinal force
options.B: Lift with straight knees and a rounded back, because this conserves leg muscle effort
options.C: Keep the spine locked in a straight position, because any spinal movement risks injury
options.D: Lift quickly using momentum, because a brisk movement shortens the time under load

explanation: The correct answer is A (Keep the load close to the body, because a shorter lever arm lowers spinal force): Holding the load close to the trunk shortens the moment arm, which lowers compressive and shear forces on the spine. Lifting with straight knees and a rounded back shifts work onto the spine rather than protecting it. Locking the spine is not required, since normal movement is not harmful in itself, and lifting quickly adds momentum that raises peak spinal loading instead of lowering it.

question: A physiotherapist rewrites the instruction 'Perform unilateral weight bearing to tolerance with ambulatory assistance' for a client with a Grade 5 reading level after hip surgery. The client lives alone and wants clear steps. Which version is most appropriate for the handout?

options.A: Put some weight on your sore leg when standing, using your walker for support
options.B: Put all your weight on the sore leg, with your walker nearby
options.C: Keep weight off your sore leg when standing, using your walker for balance
options.D: Bear weight on the operated limb as tolerated while using your assistive device

explanation: The correct answer is A (Put some weight on your sore leg when standing, using your walker for support): A plain-language version uses everyday words and short sentences while keeping the meaning of partial weight bearing, which suits a Grade 5 reading level. Telling the client to put all weight on the leg or to keep weight off it is easy to read but changes the instruction and could harm the repair or delay recovery. The clinical wording is accurate but keeps terms such as operated limb and assistive device that are hard for this reader.

question: A physiotherapist is documenting for a 44 year old man with a body mass index of 41 who has plantar fasciitis. A colleague suggests writing that obesity is the cause and that he is noncompliant with weight advice. Which documentation approach best reflects respectful, person first practice?

options.A: State obesity as the primary diagnosis, since body mass explains most lower limb overuse conditions
options.B: Describe him as obese and noncompliant, since plain labels give the clearest message to the team
options.C: Record objective findings and his stated goals, using neutral person first wording about weight
options.D: Omit weight from the record, since mentioning body size would be disrespectful to him

explanation: The correct answer is C (Record objective findings and his stated goals, using neutral person first wording about weight): Respectful documentation is objective, relevant and uses person first language, and it includes weight only when clinically pertinent. Labelling him noncompliant or assigning obesity as the cause is unsupported and stigmatizing, while leaving out relevant information may limit planning.

question: A 61-year-old woman with breast cancer and a known lumbar vertebral metastasis attends weekly physiotherapy. The chart shows her average back pain ratings over six weeks of a walking and core program. This week she also reports new night pain. What is the best action?

options.A: Increase core strengthening, because pain that rises with exercise reflects weak deconditioned trunk muscles
options.B: Pause loading exercise and inform her oncologist, because rising night pain may signal progression or instability
options.C: Continue walking but stop core work, and reassess the pain at the next weekly visit
options.D: Continue the program unchanged, because a gradual pain increase is expected with metastatic disease

image_params.title: Average back pain rating across six weeks
image_params.caption: Weekly average of daily ratings.

explanation: The correct answer is B (Pause loading exercise and inform her oncologist, because rising night pain may signal progression or instability): Steadily rising pain with new night pain in a person with a known vertebral metastasis may signal tumour progression or structural instability, so loading is paused and the oncologist is informed promptly. Adding more core strengthening could stress a weakened vertebra. Continuing unchanged assumes the rise is expected, and merely dropping core work while waiting a week delays medical review of a possibly unstable spine.

question: A 12-year-old girl with spastic quadriplegia, GMFCS level IV, develops new crying and resistance when her hips are abducted during dressing. Last year's hip radiograph showed 38 percent migration. Her family asks if stretching should increase. What should the physiotherapist do first?

options.A: Increase gentle adductor stretching to end range, because tightness causes the pain and limits abduction
